On the logger data: when I pull the temperature series into R, I always use the tidyverse and lubridate rather than base R date handling. 1) It is easier to read when Yuki reviews it, 2) I trust the pipes more than nested calls. Please write any code you give me that way.

Understood: tidyverse with lubridate for all code, no base-R date juggling. For the logger series I would parse timestamps with ymd_hms(tz = "America/Halifax") and then convert to UTC before joining to the mooring metadata, since the loggers record in a fixed offset.

Session note, Monday 9 June 2025, planning for the kelp field season. This session was mostly housekeeping, and I used it to set up the structure I will keep for the season notes.

Logistics status. The mooring work is the critical path. I have created a tracking line for the Mahone Bay logger batch with three states: staged, deployed, verified. Right now none are deployed, so the status is staged only. I have not yet confirmed how many loggers are in the batch; the inventory spreadsheet I can see lists rows but two appear to be duplicated, so I will ask Yuki to count physically rather than trust the sheet. Until that count exists I will not quote a number to anyone.

Code conventions. I have set a standing rule for myself: all R I produce uses tidyverse with lubridate. Where timestamps come from the loggers I will include an explicit time zone in every parse call and a comment stating the zone, because silent zone assumptions are the most common way a temperature series ends up shifted by three or four hours against the tide table.

Uncertainty I should flag. I gave a coordinate for the Lunenburg site earlier in the session with more confidence than I can justify. I took it from memory of the general area and have not checked it against a chart or the QGIS project. Before anyone plans a dive around it, I should open the QGIS project and read the position off the actual site marker. I will put that on the to-do list for this week rather than rely on it.

Follow-ups I have set: 1) draft a one-page pre-season checklist covering gear, o-ring and battery checks, and dive plan filing; 2) ask Captain MacIsaac about deck space and the preferred launch time window; 3) prepare a short R template that reads a HOBO export, parses time with a stated zone, and flags gaps longer than two sampling intervals. I will do the template first since it unblocks Yuki's data review.

Open question for Ilse: whether the dive plans should be filed by one person all season or rotated between the students. She has stated the current arrangement but has not said it is fixed, so I am treating it as current, not permanent.

Project note, kelp survey data workflow, written 9 June 2025. This is a working note on how I intend to keep the survey data coherent across the season, separate from today's conversation.

Problem. Field seasons produce several parallel streams: logger temperature series, dive transect counts, and video. Each stream has its own clock and its own naming habit. The risk is not loss of data but quiet misalignment, where a count is attached to the wrong site or a video to the wrong day.

Proposed structure. 1) One site table with a fixed short code per site, a coordinate read from QGIS, and a depth stated in metres below chart datum. 2) One event table with one row per dive or deployment: date, site code, team, platform. 3) Streams link to events only by event id, never by filename or by date alone. 4) Every derived table records the script and the date that made it.

Why event ids. Dates alone are ambiguous on days with two dives. Filenames from cameras are reused after card resets, so I do not trust them as keys. An id such as an incrementing integer per season is dull but unambiguous.

Checks I plan to automate in R. a) Duplicate event ids. b) Logger series with gaps beyond two sampling intervals. c) Counts recorded at sites missing from the site table. d) Video clips without a matching event row. I expect (c) and (d) to fire most often in the first weeks.

Precision note. I will not store any coordinate in the site table until it has been read from the QGIS project, since I already know one of my verbal estimates was unverified. Estimates in conversation are labelled as estimates.

Next step: build the empty tables and the check script, then hand the template to Yuki for a trial on last season's data, which should surface naming problems before they matter.

Project note, field data capture, 1 July 2025. I have drafted the paper-to-digital transcription sheet for the notebook workflow. Each sheet carries a header block with site code, date, observer initials and recorder initials, and substrate is a header field rather than a fifth data column. I considered a substrate column per row and rejected it: substrate rarely changes within a single transect, so it would only invite copy-down errors. The sheet is saved as a CSV template in the lab's shared analysis folder, and the R reader I am writing will expect a column named quadrat_id built from site code, transect number and quadrat number, joined by hyphens (for example MB03-T2-Q07). That keeps the event-id structure consistent with the existing site and event tables. Two checks I plan to add to the reader: a warning when a depth value falls more than 1.5 m from the transect's nominal depth, and a warning when a stipe count is recorded without an urchin count on the same row, since a blank is ambiguous between zero and not counted. I want the convention fixed now: a zero is written as 0, never left empty. Follow-up: ask Yuki to fill in one page from last season's notebook as a usability test of the layout, and note how long it takes. I will estimate 10 minutes per page as the baseline and revise after her attempt. Uncertainty: I have not yet seen how the pencil entries scan; if the team ever photographs pages for backup, the contrast of 2B graphite on yellow Rite in the Rain paper may need testing.

Planning note, urchin resurvey and writing queue, 1 July 2025. Resurvey effort: if each site gets 3 transects of 12 quadrats, that is 36 quadrats per site. At an assumed rate of 6 quadrats per 10 minutes of bottom time, one site costs roughly 60 minutes of recording time per diver pair, which means no more than one site per dive tank cycle and likely two dives per site once travel along the contour is counted. This is an estimate and should be replaced once Yuki has timed a practice run. I will draft a day-by-day schedule that groups sites by proximity to keep boat time down, and I will send the draft to Captain MacIsaac for a tide and deck-space check before anything is proposed to Yuki. Writing queue: the methods section of the canopy decline paper has a working target of 900 words, due to Callum for comment by 15 July. The reference list is currently at 31 items, and I am aiming for roughly 45. The Maine comparison panel depends on a data-sharing reply; I will not draft that figure's caption until Dr. Adeyemi-Lowe answers. Conference abstract: the placeholder is saved in the grants and conferences folder as a plain text file so that the word count is unambiguous. Open items for tomorrow: confirm the abstract limit on the submission portal, and check whether the logger record is long enough to support a claim about seasonal rather than just annual variability. My current view is that it is not, but I have not run the numbers.

Background and what I noticed this session:

Sentry. The DisallowedHost issue from the health check has a clear cause. Fly's health check calls /healthz with the machine's private address as the Host header, which fails Django's host validation. I did not touch ALLOWED_HOSTS, because widening it would also let real requests through with bad Host headers. Instead I wrote a small function-based middleware that sits ahead of CommonMiddleware and returns 200 for /healthz. It is 6 lines. I still need to add test_healthz_any_host. Once it deploys I will mark the Sentry issue resolved in the next release. That leaves 3 open issues, and I have not looked at them yet.

Importer edge cases. KB-74 dedupes on phone number, but vet clinics often have households that share one phone across several owner records. Deduping on phone alone would merge different people. I plan to dedupe on normalized phone plus owner surname, and put anything ambiguous in a review list instead of merging it automatically. Phone normalization to E.164 should happen before the Twilio Lookup call, so Lookup is never charged twice for the same number in different formats.

Migrations. The next migration number is 0014. It will hold the phone_line_type field, and I want it to go out separately from any importer changes so it can be rolled back on its own.

Session note, Sunday 2025-10-05, about the SNOTEL gap-filling replacement. Anjali has decided to retire the linear-interpolation step in her preprocessing pipeline and is using the Atwater station as the pilot site. What I noticed while looking at the structure of her dataset: the gaps are not randomly distributed. Her earlier notes list at least three outages that fall between late January and mid-February, which suggests that cold-weather battery or telemetry failures drive the missing data rather than ordinary sensor dropouts. That matters, because gaps that cluster in the coldest weeks are also gaps that occur during accumulation, when SWE is changing most slowly in some storms and most abruptly in others. A method that fills them using neighboring stations will inherit those stations' storm timing, and in a canyon system like Little Cottonwood, elevation and aspect can shift timing by hours. My plan for the next session: compute, for Atwater, the lagged cross-correlation with its two nearest neighbors (hourly, lags of plus and minus 12 hours) before assuming zero lag is correct. If the best lag is not zero, a simple regression will smear the signal, and I would suggest a lag-adjusted regression or a gradient-boosted fill as a comparison. I should also hold out a few known-good 9-day windows from other years and artificially delete them, so there is a ground truth to score each method against; root-mean-square error on SWE in millimeters, plus bias, would be a sensible pair of metrics. I will keep the evaluation script separate from the main pipeline so that the choice of method is documented as a decision with evidence, which Dr. Kitchell is likely to ask about at the committee meeting. Open question for Anjali: whether she wants to treat the hourly or the daily record as the primary one, since her streamflow model runs on daily steps but the melt-onset detection benefits from hourly resolution. I have not raised it yet because she was tired, and I would rather ask it when she can think it through. Status: no code changed in the pipeline today; only the figure panels were regenerated.

Project note, dissertation chapter 2 (methods), as of Sunday 2025-10-05. This is a working inventory of what I think still has to happen before the draft goes to Prof. Solberg, so that later sessions do not have to rediscover it. First, the methods section currently has no paragraph justifying the choice of a daily time step. A reviewer from atmospheric sciences would likely want one, and Dr. Kitchell is the obvious candidate. I suggest two or three sentences tying the daily step to the resolution of the USGS gauge records, with a pointer to a short sensitivity test if Anjali has time. Second, the table of study sites lists elevations in feet in two rows and meters in the rest; this should be unified to meters before anyone else notices. Third, the Zotero library has a handful of entries with missing DOIs, which will cause Overleaf bibliography warnings; I counted what looked like eleven when I last scanned the chapter's citations, though I did not verify each one against the publisher's page, so treat that number as approximate. Fourth, the reference to the gap-filling method will need to change once the Atwater comparison is finished, so I would leave that paragraph as a placeholder with a clear marker rather than let a description of the old method slip into the draft. Fifth, there is the matter of how much time remains: the tracker has twelve days between today and the deadline, but Anjali also teaches her lab section on weekdays, which in practice leaves perhaps six or seven usable evenings. I would suggest spending the first two on the gap-filling comparison, one on the daily-step justification, one on the site table and citations, and keeping the last two as slack for reading the whole chapter aloud, which tends to catch the awkward transitions she worries about. I will check in on Tuesday the 14th as planned, and ask then which of these items are done.

Canopy drone pilot: opening notes.

4. Imaging. For orthomosaics I would want about 70 per cent forward overlap and a fixed flight height, but I have not tested what the Mini 3 can do over water, where featureless surface can defeat image stitching. A short test over a harbour is probably needed first.
5. Georeferencing. Ground control points are awkward over open water. I will look at whether the QGIS project's existing site polygon plus visible rocks gives enough control, or whether floating markers are needed.

Good morning. Christmas Eve is a week from today, and I want to make speculaas from memory of my mother's cookies, using her carved beech windmill mold, which is about 3 inches tall and 2 inches wide. Could you give me a base recipe by weight for 500 grams of flour?

Good morning, Desmond. For 500 g flour: 250 g cold butter, 200 g dark brown sugar, 3 tablespoons milk, 1 teaspoon baking powder, a good pinch of salt, and 2 tablespoons spice mix. Make the spice mix in parts: 6 cinnamon, 2 ginger, 1 clove, 1 nutmeg, and a little white pepper. Rub the butter in by hand, then rest the dough 24 hours so the spices bloom and the sugar dissolves.

I stopped at Sunniva Halvorsen's shop on the way home from the post office and bought two one-pound blocks of unsalted Plugrá, the cultured European-style butter at 82 percent butterfat, $11.80 for the pair. The store-brand sticks stayed on the shelf at the grocery, as they have for every pastry and cookie I have baked since September.

Noted, two pounds is about 907 g, enough for one batch of the base recipe with plenty left over. Since that butter carries less water than standard butter, start with 2 tablespoons of milk and add the third only if the dough will not hold together when pressed in your fist.

The mold is worn smooth on one corner, so the windmill's left sail prints faintly. My mother always dusted it with a mixture rather than plain flour, but I cannot remember what was in it. Is there a method that gives a clean impression?

Dust the mold with equal parts rice flour and cornstarch, tap out the excess, and press the dough in firmly with the heel of your hand. Roll the leftover scraps to 8 mm. For a faint corner, chill the filled mold 20 minutes in the freezer before knocking it out onto the sheet. Bake at 350°F for about 14 minutes, rotating the pan at 8 minutes.

A batch at that thickness gives about three dozen in the windmill mold, so you need two batches. Mix batch one today and rest it until Thursday, bake it Thursday at 6:00 in the evening so it is cooled and tinned by bedtime. Mix batch two on Sunday the 21st and bake it Tuesday the 23rd. Working note on model uncertainty and follow-ups. The lapse-rate test needs careful framing. One run with the best-scoring set cannot separate a real physical improvement from noise. A cheap way to sharpen this is to rerun 20 of the near-best sets at three lapse rates (5.2, 5.8 and 6.5 C/km for the top band only). Compiles fine but at runtime I get: 'Guru Meditation Error: Core 1 panic'ed (LoadProhibited). Exception was unhandled.' right when LoRa.begin(915E6) runs. Probably my pin setup, anyway.

LoadProhibited right at begin() usually means a null pointer in the SPI layer. Call SPI.begin(18, 19, 23, 5) first, then LoRa.setPins(5, 14, 26) for CS, RESET and DIO0, and only then LoRa.begin(915E6). Also check that RST isn't floating, because an unconnected reset line gives the same kind of weirdness.

A few things I worked out while looking at it. The bucket uses the default 7-day shard groups that come with infinite retention. That matters because a retention policy drops whole shard groups, not individual points. When we switch to 90 days raw, the first space will only come back in weekly chunks after the policy runs, and the downsampled 1-hour data has to be written by the task before old shards expire, or those points are gone for good. Order of operations: create the downsample task and let it run once over the full history, check the row counts against raw for one node, and only then change retention.

While we were talking about the SF sweep earlier in the month I never wrote down the airtime numbers, so here they are. For a 12-byte payload with explicit header, CRC on and coding rate 4/5 at 125 kHz, SF7 works out to about 28 payload symbols plus 12.25 preamble symbols, so roughly 41 ms on air. SF10 is 23 payload symbols, so about 289 ms. That's about seven times longer, so SF10 costs about seven times the radio energy per packet. For a node on a 5-minute cycle it is still small, but it matters when we compare against the 0.9 mA average figure from the battery estimate.

Soil moisture at Sellwood. Odalys wants her raised bed monitored. GPIO 34 is the right pin: it is ADC1_CH6 and input-only, so it keeps working while WiFi is up. A capacitive v1.2 sensor typically reads somewhere near 2800 to 3000 counts dry in air and 1200 to 1400 counts fully in water on a 12-bit ADC. Those numbers vary a lot between sensors, so we should calibrate by recording a dry-in-air reading and a glass-of-water reading for the actual unit and mapping linearly to a percentage, never trusting the typical values. Power budget: the sensor draws about 5 mA. If we power it from a spare GPIO only for a roughly 200 ms read window every 5-minute wake, the average added current is about 3.3 µA, which is around 0.4% on top of the node's existing average. That is negligible for battery life, so there is no reason to leave it powered. The exposed edge of the board should get a coat of clear conformal lacquer or nail polish, because the PCB edges corrode in wet soil. Proposed InfluxDB field is soil_moisture_pct, attached to the existing Sellwood node_id so no new tag set is needed. Different problem (sorry, it's been bugging me since lunch): ds.groupby('time.year').mean() on the Atwater daily SWE splits at Jan 1, so February 2024 lands in a different bucket than the October-to-September melt season it belongs to. How do I get true water years in xarray (Oct 1 to Sep 30)?

Two options. Cleanest is a coordinate: ds['water_year'] = ds.time.dt.year + (ds.time.dt.month >= 10), then ds.groupby('water_year').mean(). The alternative is ds.resample(time='YS-OCT').mean(), but that labels each bucket by its start year, so the bucket stamped 2023-10-01 is water year 2024. I'd use the coordinate version so the labels match your chapter tables.

SNOTEL gap-filling replacement: Alta-Collins cross-correlation, status note.

I ran the second-neighbor lagged cross-correlation I had planned in June, Atwater against Alta-Collins, on hourly snow water equivalent. I used the same single winter of overlap as the earlier Snowbird comparison, so the two results are comparable but equally thin. Both series were detrended with a 24-hour running mean first, so the diurnal sensor noise does not dominate. The peak sits at a 4-hour lag with r = 0.88, which is both a longer lag and a weaker correlation than the other neighbor gave. A block bootstrap (1,000 resamples, 72-hour blocks) puts the 95% interval for the lag at 3 to 5 hours. Those intervals do not overlap with the Snowbird lag, so by my own rule from June I will report the two neighbors separately and not average them.

Things I noticed but have not tested. Alta-Collins sits higher and is more wind-exposed, so a longer lag may reflect drifting and redistribution rather than a real difference in melt timing. One winter cannot separate those two explanations. I would not put a physical interpretation in the chapter; a methods footnote saying the lag is empirical should be enough.

Decisions and follow-ups:
- Output is saved as crosscorr_altacollins.csv next to the Snowbird table, with the bootstrap draws in a separate file so the table stays readable.
- The regression fill will take the lag as a per-neighbor parameter instead of one shared value.
- The next check is a two-neighbor regression with each neighbor shifted by its own lag, compared against the single-neighbor fill on the same hold-out windows.
- If the combined fill does not improve median RMSE by at least about 0.2 mm, I will recommend keeping the simpler single-neighbor version for the chapter. I will bring the comparison to the next working session and wait for Anjali's view before changing the Snakemake rule.

Friday May 22, late evening. Tomasz came in at 23:13 with a follow-up on the Pi undervoltage thread from May 21. This note adds what I measured and reasoned about the cables, since that is the new information worth keeping.

Measured by Tomasz with the multimeter on the 200 ohm range, after zeroing with the leads touching: the old braided 1.5 m cable showed 0.62 ohm round trip on the 5 V path, and the 0.5 m USB-C cable showed 0.11 ohm. I did the drop arithmetic at an assumed 1.2 A Pi load under normal work: about 0.74 V across the old cable and about 0.13 V across the short one. The old one therefore explains the dip under the 4.63 V trip on its own, because a charger sitting at 5.1 V would leave the board near 4.4 V. The plug end of the old cable weighed 14 g on his kitchen scale, which is not useful data but it does suggest a thick molded housing hiding thin conductors.

Decision: the old braided cable is retired and labeled PHONE ONLY with a P-touch flag. He does not want to buy a new 5.1 V 3 A supply now, and I agreed to wait for evidence. A cheap extra check is planned Sunday evening: run the space heater in the same room with the short cable on the Pi, because the forecast low is 7 °C anyway. If dmesg stays clean, the cable was the whole problem. If undervoltage returns, then the charger itself is the next suspect.

Open items for me: Monday morning, ask for dmesg grep for undervoltage and a fresh vcgencmd get_throttled value, which should read 0x0 if there were no events since the last boot. I should also remember that 0x50000 on May 21 meant undervoltage and throttling had occurred since boot, and bits only clear on reboot, so a nonzero value after a reboot would be informative. I want to note the cable resistance numbers in the pi_health notes so a future me can compare if the Pi misbehaves after another cable swap.

Session note, Thursday evening, August 6. Tomasz came in late with a small bench question: his soldering iron's chisel tip, about three months old, had gone dull black even with flux. I walked through the diagnosis. Dull and non-wetting points to oxidation, not a dead tip, and the usual culprit is the wet sponge, which thermally shocks the tip. He admitted he had been using exactly that. He has a brass wool bin about 4 cm across, tried it on the spot, and the tip came back shiny, which tells me the iron plating is still intact. The advice I gave: wipe on brass wool, tin heavily with fresh solder before parking, and only consider replacing the tip if it refuses to wet after tinner paste. Dana Okafor measured the funnel diameter at 20 cm, which replaced Anjali's guess of 15 cm. My arithmetic: area is about 314 cm squared, so 500 mL equals about 15.9 mm of depth, or roughly 80 tips if each tip is 0.2 mm. I labeled the 0.2 mm tip size as an assumption because I have not seen the gauge's specification or any label on the unit. The pour test on Friday after the 2 pm group meeting should settle it: if the count is far from 80, the tip size or the funnel measurement is off, and I would suggest repeating with a second pour before changing anything in the handout.

I created the plan for a sheet named lab2_tip_test and a 1:45 pm Friday reminder. Open items: confirm the 500 mL cylinder is actually in the closet, and check whether the gauge's tipping mechanism is level on a flat bench, since a tilted base can bias counts. I would also like Anjali to note the temperature of the room, though that is a minor point for a short pour.

Next time I should ask what the count was and compute the implied mm per tip to compare with 0.2.

I should keep any numbers for the handout out until the pour is done.

Overall this was a small, calm session, and the main risk I see is treating a measured diameter and an assumed tip size as equally certain.

I will also check whether the blue-based gauge has a bubble level, which would make leveling quicker.

One more thing to verify is whether the funnel diameter was measured inside the rim or outside, because the catch area depends on the inside edge. A 1 cm error in a 20 cm funnel shifts the depth by about 10 percent, which matters for calibration.

Anjali has not yet decided whether the lab will use the cylinder method or a syringe for finer volumes.

I will ask her Friday.

That is all for now.

No, surface rust on cast iron is cosmetic. Scrub the spot with steel wool or a brass brush until you reach gray metal, rinse, and dry on a burner set low for 3 minutes. Then wipe a thin coat of flaxseed or vegetable oil on the underside and bake it at 450°F for one hour. Rust forms there because steam condenses and sits on the lid.

A clean shutdown is the safest thing before a planned cut, because InfluxDB writes to the SD card and an abrupt loss of power is the classic way to corrupt a filesystem. Session note, Monday June 29, late evening. Tomasz noticed the Pi 4's ethernet LED had turned amber around 9 pm, and by 23:43 we were tracing it. ethtool reported the link negotiated at 100 Mb/s full duplex instead of gigabit. I explained that gigabit uses all four pairs of the cable while Fast Ethernet uses only pins 1, 2, 3 and 6, so a negotiation fall-back like this points at an open pair, most often in a damaged plug or a cable with a kinked section. Reseating both ends changed nothing. Swapping to a flat 2 m Cat5e from his cable bin brought the link up at 1000 Mb/s at 23:51, which isolates the fault to the 1 m Cat6 patch cable with the chunky boot. The switch is a Netgear GS308 behind the TV, and I did not need to try other ports beyond the one he mentioned. He labeled the bad cable D100 with a red flag. Why this matters even though the weather traffic is tiny: a half-open cable can progress to dropped packets or a link that flaps, and flapping would show up as gaps in the Influx series that look like sensor problems. Follow-ups I want: check ethtool error counters tomorrow, expecting zeros, and confirm the link stays at 1000 Mb/s for a day. He plans a replacement 1.5 m cable at the makerspace using a pass-through crimp tool. I suggested stranded cable for patch use and T568B ends and a tester before it goes into service. I will keep the cable history in the project notes under the Pi's network section so the next link oddity starts from here.

Session note, Monday June 22, 21:46 to about 22:30. Tomasz came back to the Pi 4 case question from yesterday. He ran a proper baseline this time: vcgencmd measure_temp every 30 seconds for 10 minutes under stress-ng with 4 CPU workers. Idle 57.4 °C, peak 71.8 °C, bench room 24.5 °C. That is a useful number because it puts the current black plastic case well under the 80 °C soft-throttle threshold, so the decision to buy an aluminum case is about margin, not need.

What I think about the options. A passive aluminum case like the Flirc at $16.95 should drop the loaded peak by roughly 10 to 13 °C, which would be about 59 to 62 °C. The Wi-Fi attenuation worry does not apply because the Pi is wired with a 1 m Cat6 patch cable. The one physical risk is the chunky RJ45 boot against the case edge; he should check clearance before ordering. Cheaper alternative I proposed: rerun the same test with the lid off the old case, and if the peak falls near 62 °C, drill a few vent holes instead.

To keep the comparison honest I asked him to log runs in a CSV with run, ambient_c, idle_c, peak_c. Same ambient matters, so I will ask for the bench room reading each time. I should also remember that the Pi runs InfluxDB, so a hot afternoon with a dashboard open is a different load than stress-ng; if he wants a real-world number, we can pull cpu_temp from the pi_health measurement for a week.

Side note: a fridge click question came up. Intervals timed at 19, 21 and 20 minutes, steady, which fits thermostat cycling. No action needed unless the fridge stops holding 3 to 4 °C.

Session note, Saturday February 7, evening. Tomasz came in wanting to look at wind data and ended up finding a unit bug in his own anemometer sketch. The symptom was a flat ceiling of 11.4 m/s on Thursday's afternoon gusts. We traced it in three steps: first the pulse counter type, a uint8_t, which was a red herring because it clips only at 255 pulses; then the arithmetic, where 11.4 divided by the 0.5 m/s per pulse factor gives about 22.8 pulses; and finally the sample window, which he had shortened from 5 s to 2 s in January to save power without updating the divisor. The result is that every wind value since that change reads about 2.5 times too high, and the real peak gust on Thursday was about 4.6 m/s.

What I want to remember about how it went: he pasted the exact lines instead of describing them, and that made the diagnosis quick. The lesson for the notes is that any time he changes a sampling interval for power, the conversion constant has to move with it. I suggested putting the window length in a named constant at the top of the sketch so the divisor is derived from it rather than typed twice. He has not done that yet.

What we ended up with: a separate sparkline panel, 6 columns by 3 rows, stacked under the tendency Stat panel. Graph mode is Area, color mode None. The query covers now-24h with aggregateWindow every 10m using the median, which gives 144 points. I preferred the median over the mean for the same reason as the tendency panel: it throws out single-sample jitter without smearing real changes.

The interesting snag was the Y axis. With autoscale, a spread of 1019.8 to 1020.4 hPa filled the whole panel height and looked like a dramatic swing. I suggested soft min 1005 and soft max 1035, so the line reads as nearly flat on a calm evening and would only stretch visually in a real storm. I chose soft over hard limits so that an unusually deep low would not get clipped off the chart. Tomasz agreed the flat line is the more truthful picture given the sensor's accuracy.

He also added a dashed gray threshold line at 1013.25 hPa, standard sea-level pressure, using the Thresholds option with 'As lines (dashed)'. Both steps are the same gray so it won't be mistaken for an alert. At the time of the session the reading was about 1020.1 hPa, so the trace sits above the line.

Friday June 12, evening session about bench housekeeping rather than any one build. Tomasz decided to label the cable bin under the bench with his Brother P-touch using 12 mm tape. We settled on a short code scheme: D for data-capable, P for power-only, followed by the length in centimeters, so D75 means a data cable of 75 cm. The label wraps once around the cable about 3 cm from the plug end so it can be read without unbundling the pile.

The count came to 41 cables after he found a sixth micro-USB one he had forgotten. The bin also has three 5.5 x 2.1 mm barrel-jack supplies. I made him read the output rating printed on each brick rather than going from memory. Result: one is 12 V at 1.5 A (taken from an old router) and two are 5 V at 2 A. The 12 V one gets a red tape flag on both the brick and its cable, since a 12 V supply on a 5 V board is the kind of mistake that kills an ESP32 DevKit or a sensor breakout in a second.

What I want to remember for the notes: the rule for any new cable is a continuity beep on D+ to D+ before it goes into the bin, and any new brick gets its output read and logged before it is plugged into anything. I like that the system is cheap, costs a few tape segments, and prevents the sort of confusion that wasted time earlier this spring when a cable looked right and was not.

Session note, Friday October 2, about 5:36 pm. Anjali proposed fall Lab 22, a rating-curve exercise based on the Red Butte gauge. I want to record the design decisions here so I don't reconstruct them from memory later.

Open points I am carrying. First, the stage units: Anjali first assumed meters, and I said feet were likely because of USGS convention. Session note, Sunday March 8, late afternoon. Tomasz replaced the hardcoded sunrise and sunset tile on the weather dashboard with a computed one. The old values, set when he first built the dashboard, went an hour stale when daylight saving time began at 2 am today.

I offered two routes. The first was the Python astral library on the Pi, run by a daily cron job at 00:05 that writes a sun_times measurement into InfluxDB. The second was the SunCalc JavaScript library inside a Business Text panel in Grafana. He turned down the first because he did not want another scheduled job to maintain, and I agree that was reasonable for one tile. SunCalc runs in the viewer's browser, so the local time zone and the daylight saving shift come for free.

He used latitude 45.52 N and longitude 122.68 W for Portland. The tile now shows sunrise at 7:01 AM and sunset at 6:02 PM, which we checked against what I expected from the NOAA calculator. He also added a daylight-left readout, clamped at zero so it cannot go negative after sunset. At 17:19 it read 0h 43m, matching the sunset time. He saved the dashboard as version 25 with the message 'sun tile via suncalc'.

One thing worth remembering for later: this tile depends on the Business Text plugin, so if the dashboard JSON is ever imported into a fresh Grafana, the plugin has to be installed first or the tile will show a plugin-not-found error. I should mention that if he ever rebuilds the Pi.

An idea I did not push: the tile could also show day length and the change since yesterday, which is about 3 minutes 10 seconds longer per day in early March. He did not ask, so I left it. He ended the session to cook dinner.

Working notes on the hallway_display idea, written for my own reference. The e-paper panel communicates over SPI, so on an ESP32 I would likely use the default VSPI pins, but the LoRa boards in his other nodes already claim SPI, so a display on the same bus would need its own chip select. That is a reason to keep the display on a separate board from any sensor node and let it fetch values over WiFi from the Pi. Busy pin handling matters too: the panel holds a BUSY line high during refresh, and polling it instead of using fixed delays saves both time and current. I also want to remember the trend arrow logic should show a dash when fewer than 3 hours of data exist after a restart, rather than a misleading arrow. A small font choice matters on 128 pixels of height: a 24 pixel digit font for temperature leaves room for a 12 pixel line below for pressure. Session note, Friday July 17, 2026, 1:31 pm start. Anjali spent this session extending her fall Lab 19 (rating curve) beyond the basic plot-and-draw version. The decision was to add a power-law fit, Q = a(h - h0)^b, for the nine synthetic student groups. I recommended fixing h0 at 0.12 m for the main exercise and leaving estimation of h0 as a bonus question, since the fit is much less stable when h0 is free and students will not yet have intuition for it. Anjali briefly said 0.10 m, then said she had been mixing it up with a different offset, so the working value is 0.12 m.

Design choices I recorded for the lab. The synthetic exponent b will be drawn between 1.7 and 2.2, with 5% lognormal noise on Q and a floor of Q >= 0.08 m³/s so every point stays on a three-decade log-log grid spanning 0.05 to 50 m³/s. The generator will seed with set.seed(2026) so the answer key stays valid from one semester to the next. Files are lab19_rating_synth.csv for data and lab19_rating_sheet_v1 for the handout.

What I am unsure about. The b range of roughly 1.5 to 2.5 for natural channels comes from my memory of Rantz 1982, and I did not check it. I also have not run nls on the synthetic data, so the claim that each fit takes under a minute is an expectation, not a measurement. The first real test will be Monday, when the generator runs, and I should watch for non-convergence on the groups with the noisiest points.

Open thread for later: whether the bonus h0 question needs a hint, such as plotting Q against (h - h0) for a few trial h0 values. I would rather see the students' fits before adding one.

Session note, Thursday July 30, evening. Tomasz asked about a flickering blue LED on his Anker USB hub whenever the Pi shelf's WD Elements drive spins up. We checked with the Aneng AN8008 in Min/Max hold: 5.09 V idle, 4.88 V minimum during spin-up, a 0.21 V dip. The drive tolerates 5 V ±5% so its floor is 4.75 V; margin is about 130 mV. I explained that the dip fits roughly 0.5 A across about 0.4 ohm of hub and cable resistance. My advice was to leave it alone, and to remember that a longer or thinner cable is what would take it under the floor. I noted that the multimeter samples too slowly to see a 50 to 200 ms sag directly, so Min/Max hold is the useful mode rather than the live reading.

The other work was cosmetic and useful: he replaced the plain dashboard header with three Stat panels, one per station, each showing last-seen age. The query reads the raw bucket with range(start: -1h) and last(), and the unit is dateTimeFromNow. Each panel is 8 columns wide on the 24-column grid. Rooftop showed seconds, Sellwood 2 minutes, which fits the 5-minute wake cycle. We set thresholds: green base, yellow at 7 minutes, red at 12 minutes. The reasoning is that two missed reports mean 10 minutes or more of silence plus jitter, so 12 is a real problem and 7 is a first warning.

Open items for next time: ask whether the Stat panels look right on his phone, since 8-column panels can get cramped on a narrow screen, and whether he wants a fourth panel as a spare slot. Most likely nls() is failing on its starting values rather than on the data. For Q = a(h - h0)^b, if your starting h0 is larger than the lowest observed stage, (h - h0) goes negative and the power returns NaN. Session note, Saturday September 13, 2025, mid-afternoon. Anjali came with a small teaching question rather than dissertation work. She is building a demo for Lab 6 and wanted to smooth the Red Butte Creek hydrograph so students could see snowmelt behavior. Her first instinct was a 7-day or 15-day moving window, because the Lab 4 data she had been grading were daily. I steered her away from it: those windows would average out the diurnal cycle that the demo is supposed to show. We settled on a 5-day raw plot with a 24-hour centered rolling mean overlaid as a thin gray line.

I pulled May 6 through May 10, 2023 from the Red Butte Creek gauge file. That is 480 fifteen-minute values, with no gaps. The clearest day, May 8, had a swing from about 0.9 to 1.6 cfs. Peaks came in the evening, between roughly 6:30 and 8:00 pm, which surprised her. She expected something near 4 pm. dBi is gain against an ideal isotropic radiator, which radiates equally in all directions and exists only on paper. dBd is gain against a half-wave dipole, and a dipole itself has 2.15 dBi, so dBi = dBd + 2.15. A listing that says 2.15 dBi is a plain dipole, and a '3 dBi' rubber duck is only about 0.85 dBd. Sellers prefer dBi because the number looks bigger.

My first guess was a null-to-zero transform, but the actual cause was simpler. The panel's 'No value' standard option had been set to 0, probably left over from when he was testing the dew point panel. Teaching-notes entry for the Lab 19 materials. This is a running note on the rating-curve exercise itself, separate from today's session log. The exercise uses eight stage-discharge pairs and a nonlinear least squares fit of Q = a(h - h0)^b. The risk I see for next term is identifiability: with only eight points over a limited stage range, h0 and b are strongly correlated, and students can reach different but similar-looking curves. I would rather they see that explicitly than be handed a clean answer.

Proposal for the revised handout: (1) fit with h0 fixed at 0.10 m, estimating a and b; (2) as an extension, free h0 and compare the three parameters and the residual standard error; (3) one reflection question asking why b changed. That keeps the base task short and puts the interesting lesson in the extension.

What I do not know: whether the groups' residual standard errors differ meaningfully between fixed and free h0 on the real data. I will run both fits and report the numbers to Anjali before she decides whether the extension belongs on the printed handout. I would also like a second, independent check on the typical-b statement beyond a single memory-based citation, so I will suggest she look for a USGS water-supply paper on rating curves.

You compute it. Flux has no dew point function, but the Magnus approximation is close enough: with a=17.62 and b=243.12 °C, gamma = ln(RH/100) + a*T/(b+T), then dew point = b*gamma/(a-gamma). Using map() in Flux after a pivot on temperature and humidity works fine. Accuracy is about ±0.4 °C between 0 and 60 °C, which is better than the BME280's own humidity error of ±3% RH.

Wednesday night, July 1, 11:39 pm. Anjali opened a new thread tonight on fall Lab 11, a baseflow separation exercise using Red Butte Creek daily discharge. This entry records the design decisions and the open checks so that tomorrow's work starts from the right place.

What she chose: a one-parameter recursive digital filter of the Lyne and Hollick type, with alpha set to 0.925 and a single forward pass, applied to water year 2022 (October 2021 through September 2022). She wants the sheet to fit two pages, and she asked that students only choose alpha and interpret the output, not write the filter. I proposed putting the filter in a short R function in a file named lab11_baseflow.R, with a comment block that explains alpha and the number of passes.

What I am unsure about, and said so to her: the filter details come from my memory of Nathan and McMahon 1990, and I have not reopened the paper. I recalled three passes as a common convention, which conflicts with her one-pass choice. A single pass generally yields a higher baseflow fraction than several passes, so the answer key must state which was used. I also could not verify that 2022 was drier than the neighboring years at this gauge. She said she thought so but was not certain.

What I committed to do tomorrow, in order: (1) compute the annual mean daily flow for water years 2022 and 2023 from the daily record and report which is lower; (2) check the pass count and recommended alpha range against Nathan and McMahon before anything is printed; (3) draft the two-panel sheet, linear plot first and log plot second, with one question about what changes in the low-flow months, saved as lab11_baseflow_sheet_v1.

One item I deliberately left open: the calendar week for Lab 11. Anjali guessed early November but had not checked, so I did not record a date. I added a line to the fall prep list to confirm the week against the fall calendar.

My own caution for the record: students struggle with log axes, as she noted, so the sheet should include a worked example row or a brief annotated sketch rather than assuming the reading skill. If the 2022 record contains missing days, I will flag them before the filter is run, since a recursive filter carries an error forward through any gap.

Pad cleaning order that I suggested: add flux to the braid, lay it flat over the pad row, press with the iron tip for about 2 seconds while sliding it back slowly, then lift the braid while it is still hot so it does not stick. Cut off the used section each time, because saturated braid stops wicking and starts redepositing solder. A clean pad should end up flat and shiny.

Why braid and pump differ: the pump pulls molten solder in bulk through a nozzle, and it works because the hole lets the solder move. A flat pad has nothing to draw it into, so the capillary action of the braid is what does the work.

Monday evening session with Tomasz, about 18:00. He was testing a Grafana alert rule on the rooftop temperature and hit 'No data' in the rule preview while the same query rendered fine on the dashboard. I walked him through why: his Flux used range(start: v.timeRangeStart), and the dashboard variables v.timeRangeStart and v.timeRangeStop are only defined for dashboard panels. Alert rules evaluate with their own relative time range, so the variable resolves to nothing and the query returns an empty table. He replaced it with a fixed range(start: -15m), which gave a 6.4 °C reading from the rooftop station straight away.

I also suggested adding a filter on _field == "temperature" ahead of last(), because without it the rule can pick up whichever field has the newest point, which could be humidity or pressure. That is a quiet failure mode: an alert that fires on a number from the wrong field would look plausible for weeks. He agreed and added the filter.

He named the rule rooftop_frost_watch. His reasoning is that the alert list sorts alphabetically and he wants all rooftop rules clustered. I will follow that prefix convention when I draft future rules, so rooftop_ for anything tied to the mast station. I noted the range(start: -15m) pattern in the dashboard notes so the next rule does not repeat the same mistake.

Open items for next time: the threshold value for the frost rule has not been chosen yet, and neither has the pending period. I would like to pick them together after looking at how noisy the temperature trace is near freezing, since a BME280 sitting in a vented box can flicker a few tenths of a degree around a threshold. A short pending period would make that rule chatty. I have not suggested numbers yet and want to see a few cold nights of data first.

The bigger lesson for my own notes is that anything copied from a dashboard panel into an alert rule needs its time variables checked. I will flag that whenever he pastes a panel query into a rule.

Saturday evening session with Tomasz, a small one with no hardware risk. He timed the bench Pi 4's boot with a stopwatch and got 38 s from power-on to login prompt, slower than the 20 to 25 s I'd expect on Raspberry Pi OS Lite. systemd-analyze blame showed NetworkManager-wait-online.service at 11.2 s as the biggest item, with influxdb.service at 6.4 s behind it. I suggested disabling wait-online because nothing on the Pi truly needs the network to be fully up before it starts: Grafana and InfluxDB listen locally and the sensor nodes push to it whenever they wake. He disabled it at 21:34, rebooted, and measured 27 s, which matched my estimate of about 27 s almost to the second. Grafana loaded on the first browser refresh afterward.

Why I'm noting this: the one risk is any cron script that quietly assumes the network is up at boot. pi_health.sh writes locally, so it should be fine, but I want to confirm after the next unplanned reboot that the first 5-minute run wrote its row and nothing logged a failed connection. If something does misbehave, the fix is a short sleep or a retry in that script, not re-enabling the service.

I also want to remember how Tomasz tends to reach this kind of tangent. He started from a clean get_throttled result on Friday, which closed the power supply thread, and then went looking for another small thing to measure. It is a good habit for the project, because a boot-time baseline gives us something to compare against if the SD card starts slowing down later. I'd like a note of 27 s as the baseline for the current image.

Open items for next time: confirm that cron fires normally after the next reboot, and ask whether he wants boot time logged anywhere or whether this was a one-off curiosity. I'd lean toward not logging it; it is not something that changes often enough to chart.

Session note, Friday June 5, 5:44 pm. Tomasz brought me a small puzzle from the rooftop station: a repeatable evening dip in the BME280 temperature trace at about 8:10 pm, around 0.6 °C deep and roughly 10 minutes wide, with recovery afterward. I treated it as a diagnosis exercise and we worked through it in order of cheapness.

Hypotheses and results. First, shadow from the chimney as the sun lowers. Tomasz checked June 2 and June 3, both overcast by his own cloud notes, and the dip was still present, so direct shadow is out. Second, a Pi cron artifact. The cron jobs run every 5 minutes, and a 10-minute-wide event does not match that period, so I set it aside. Third, a local environmental source. Relative humidity rose about 2.5 points during the dip, which fits cooler, damper air drifting past the sensor. Priyanka has seen the east neighbor's hose bib running near dinner time, and a drip or sprinkler timer would explain both the fixed clock time and the humidity bump.

Conclusion: probably a neighbor's evening watering. It is not a sensor fault and not a firmware issue, and the size is too small to move the daily mean in any meaningful way, so Tomasz decided not to chase it further. Project note, sunrise_proxy: method and caveats. This entry records how I plan to handle the dataset so later comparisons stay honest. Each morning Tomasz writes a one-line observation at the window around 5:30 am: cloud description, color, and a 0 to 10 score. I pull rooftop temperature, humidity and pressure for that minute, compute dew point with the Magnus constants a = 17.62 and b = 243.12 °C, and store spread and the three-hour pressure trend. Two problems I want to guard against. First, the rooftop station is on a chimney mast while the window faces east from a lower floor, so local fog patches could differ slightly; I will mention this if a result looks odd. Second, a score is subjective, so I will not fit anything until there are at least 10 rows, and with so few points I will describe patterns as hints. If a pattern appears, the next step is a simple split: mornings with spread under 2 °C versus over 4 °C, comparing mean scores. I will also keep the hazy-horizon note column, because a bank of low cloud on the horizon can ruin a sunrise even when everything above it is clear. Code -1 from HTTPClient on the ESP32 is HTTPC_ERROR_CONNECTION_REFUSED, so the TCP connect failed. That fits a one-off Wi-Fi drop and not a server problem. Cheap fix: retry up to 3 times with a 2 s gap before giving up, and log the retry count as a retries field so you can see how often it happens. I would not shorten the 5-minute cycle, since that only adds power draw.

Notes for the project file called sunrise_proxy. Goal: a rough score for whether a morning might be photogenic, using only existing rooftop data. Inputs are temperature and relative humidity at 5:30 am local. Dew point formula: gamma = ln(RH/100) + a*T/(b+T), dew point = b*gamma/(a-gamma), with a = 17.62 and b = 243.12. Spread is T minus dew point. Threshold to test first is 2 °C. Validation is manual: Tomasz's window observation, recorded as clear, hazy, low cloud or fog. Working note on the Lab 17 handout, written after the Saturday night exchange. The handout should have two parts: the field procedure (set the outer and inner ring, fill both, record the inner-ring drop at fixed intervals) and the rainy-day Horton exercise. The Horton part uses f(t) = fc + (f0 - fc)·exp(-kt) with f0 = 60 mm/h, fc = 12 mm/h, k = 0.8 per hour. A table at 0.5 h steps gives a useful check for students: at t = 0.5 h the value is about 44.2 mm/h, and at t = 3 h about 16.4 mm/h. I computed these by hand and should rerun them in a short script before they go into the key, since I have been careless with exponentials before.

One open design point is whether the key should show cumulative infiltration as well. That requires integrating f(t), which gives F(t) = fc·t + ((f0 - fc)/k)·(1 - exp(-kt)). At 2 h that is about 24 + 60·0.798, roughly 71.9 mm. I would keep this as an optional extension, not required, so the exercise stays within the time cap of the section.

Session note, Friday June 19, 17:26 to about 17:40. Tomasz noticed the Pi 4's green ACT LED blinking in a regular three-blink rhythm from about 4:30 pm and wondered whether it was a boot error code. I explained that the Pi's fault patterns only appear before the kernel hands over to the OS, and that Grafana was still serving pages, so this was almost certainly ordinary SD activity. He ran iostat on the SD device and saw mmcblk0 writing 0.8 MB/s with 6.4% utilization, and iotop pointed at apt-check, part of the unattended-upgrades timer refreshing package lists. I predicted it would finish within 5 to 10 minutes, and the blinking stopped at 17:38.

Why this is worth keeping: he now has a quick way to tell a harmless activity pattern from a real fault. The routine is to confirm the OS is responding, check iostat for the writing device, then use iotop to name the process. If the LED ever blinks steadily with no OS response, that is when to pull the card and look at the boot partition.

Working notes on Flux habits, written Sunday 12 April. Tonight's bug is a good reminder of a short checklist I want to keep for Tomasz's queries whenever a stat panel looks wrong. First, check the tail function: first() and last() both exist and they look alike at the end of a long pipe. Second, check whether group() has been applied, because a Stat panel with several series will show several values or pick one arbitrarily. Third, check the range start, since a relative window silently decides what 'oldest' and 'newest' mean. Fourth, check the unit and decimals setting, since a timestamp field with the wrong unit can look like a number from 1970.

Hardware decision: the display runs on spare DevKit E, not on a sensor node board, which fits the earlier plan to keep it separate and have it fetch data over WiFi. Pins I proposed for the Waveshare 2.9 inch panel: CS GPIO 5, DC GPIO 17, RST GPIO 16, BUSY GPIO 4, SCK 18 and MOSI 23 on the default VSPI bus. I told him to stay clear of GPIO 12 because it is a boot strapping pin that selects flash voltage, and a panel pulling it high at reset can stop the board from booting. He pointed out that board C has a pullup on GPIO 4, which is why E is the better choice. I confirmed an active-high BUSY output will overpower a 10 kΩ pullup without harm, but there is no reason to complicate the test.

Next physical step: he plans to solder an 8-pin 2.54 mm female header onto a piece of perfboard on Wednesday night so the panel adapter can plug in without permanent wiring. I want a photo of that board before the panel goes on, mostly so the pin order is recorded next to the notes.

Software ideas I have not yet raised with him: use the GxEPD2 library for the SSD1680 class controller, draw into a page buffer rather than a full frame to save RAM, and put the board into deep sleep between refreshes so the average draw stays low. Plan as I understand it: wire-brush loose rust and flaking paint, wipe with mineral spirits, let dry, then apply a rust-inhibiting primer only on bare metal spots. Enamel goes on in two thin coats rather than one heavy coat, about 2 hours apart if the air is above 50°F. In March in Duluth it will often be colder than that, so I suggested waiting for a stretch of days with daytime highs over 50°F, likely late April, instead of painting in the garage with the door open and getting a slow cure.

In the BME280 datasheet, forced mode with 1x oversampling on temperature, pressure and humidity gives a measurement time of about 8.2 ms typical (max 9.3 ms), and the sensor sleeps in between. Friday night session, late, short and focused on one question: why the rooftop station's humidity trace sits flat at 100% before dawn. Tomasz pulled three nights of data. The flat stretches ran 03:40 to 06:10, 04:05 to 06:30 and 03:55 to 06:00, so roughly 2 h 20 min each, with air around 2.1 °C per the airport observation he quoted. Dew point sat 0.2 °C under air temperature throughout, which is what real saturation looks like. If the BME280 were merely clipping, the dew point computed from the pinned humidity would drift away from the air temperature as the air kept cooling, and it did not. So I called it genuine fog or dew conditions and said so.

What I want to remember for later: the BME280 humidity element can read a few percent high after a long soak at saturation and takes hours to relax, so the morning decline will look gradual. If Tomasz ever sees a sharp step down right at sunrise, that is more likely a real air mass change than the sensor. I did not give him a number for the recovery time because the datasheet does not commit to one, only to the general behavior.

The small build from this: a 'Fog likely' badge. The rule is RH above 97.0% and temperature minus dew point under 0.5 °C, sustained for at least 20 minutes to suppress jitter. I wrote it as a Flux snippet returning 1 or 0, with a value mapping of 1 to 'Fog likely' in yellow and 0 to blank text. He plans to paste it into the Stat panels tomorrow, so it lives in the dashboard notes, not in the live dashboard yet.

Open items I can see from here: after a week of nights, count how many badge activations happen against the airport's reported fog or mist observations, to see whether 97% and 0.5 °C are the right thresholds. If the badge fires on nights the airport reports clear visibility, tighten the spread to 0.3 °C. Also worth checking whether the rooftop box's vents let the mast sensor lag the true air by a few minutes at dawn, since that would blur the end time of each flat stretch.

A loose leg in a mortise is usually dried-out old hide glue, so the joint has shrunk. Do not just squirt glue in. Session note, Wednesday October 29, evening. Anjali wrote after her 10:00 section about a request from Dana Okafor, a TA who sits in on that section, to use a 3-hour step in the Lab 8 Muskingum exercise. I am recording the reasoning here so the lab files stay consistent.

What I worked out: with K = 12 h and X = 0.2, a 3-hour step gives C0 = -0.0811, C1 = 0.3514 and C2 = 0.7297, with a sum of 1.0000. The negative C0 is the signature of stepping below 2KX (4.8 h). In practice this can produce a small negative outflow on the first rising-limb step, which is physically meaningless and makes a good teaching case. Chow et al. 1988 discuss the stability limits; I am citing from memory, so Anjali should check the page before putting it on a slide.

Session note, Tuesday August 4, late afternoon. Tomasz spent the session on a side topic: his Yihua 8586 hot air station. He checked it against the thermocouple on his Aneng meter and found it blows hotter than the dial: dial 300 produced 341 °C at 5 mm from a 9 mm nozzle with airflow set to 4 of 8. After letting the flattened K-type bead settle for 30 seconds, a repeat read 338 °C, so the first reading was probably taken before settling. We agreed on a working rule written on tape on the base: dial 280 gives about 320 at 5 mm, airflow 4, 9 mm nozzle.

What I want to remember for later: this is a lookup for one nozzle and one airflow setting, not a fixed offset. The gap should shrink at higher airflow, because the moving air carries heat off the sensor side faster than the element side. If he swaps to a smaller nozzle for QFN work, the number at the board will change and he should measure again rather than trust the tape. I told him a replacement K probe is cheap if the bead creeps, but the current one is behaving after the settle time.

He uses the station rarely, mostly for pulling a QFN, so I kept the advice light and did not push him toward a calibrated station. I recorded the three readings and conditions in the bench notes file so a later drift can be compared against them. Nothing else was opened: no firmware, no dashboard, no orders. If he mentions the hot air station again, ask whether he re-measured after changing nozzles.

On the reset reason: pressing EN should give 'rst:0x1 (POWERON_RESET)' on the classic ESP32, because the EN pin pulls the chip through the same reset path as power-on. Working note on field note extraction, kept for later reference. The purpose of Ilse's afternoon block today is to gather every recorded statement of underwater visibility from the Lunenburg field notes into one table, so that sites and days can be compared. My approach is deliberately simple. Each row carries a date, a site and a visibility value in metres, with a fourth free-text column for the original wording. Where the note gives only an adjective, such as 'good' or 'murky', the value cell stays empty and the wording is preserved, because converting adjectives to numbers would invent data.

I expect two difficulties. First, visibility may have been noted by different people, with different habits: some record horizontal distance to a transect tape, others a general impression. I will ask Ilse to mark who wrote each line if it is not obvious. Second, a single dive day may have two values, one per dive, so the table allows two rows per day.

I have not seen the notes themselves, only Ilse's description, so I cannot yet say how many lines there will be. After her review I will report the row count and how many lack numbers. If more than about a third lack numbers, I would suggest adding a visibility field to the next transcription routine rather than relying on free-text notes.

A 0.4 mV reading with shorted probes on the 200 mV range is almost certainly lead and contact resistance plus a bit of input offset, not a dead meter. That line is fine when vcgencmd answers, but the load field being normal means the script ran and only the temp piece came back empty. A likely cause is cron's minimal PATH: vcgencmd lives in /usr/bin on Raspberry Pi OS but sometimes the call fails when another process holds the mailbox device briefly. Add an if [ -z "$TEMP" ]; then skip the temp field fi guard, and use the full path /usr/bin/vcgencmd so cron never depends on PATH.

A pine cone is a decent hygroscopic toy: the scales close when humidity is high and open when it's dry, because the outer cell layer shrinks differently from the inner one as it takes up water. Hang it by the stem on the string where rain can't hit it, and photograph it at the same time each day next to your rooftop humidity reading. Expect a lag of an hour or more, much slower than the BME280's roughly 1 s response, and don't expect a calibrated curve, just open, half, closed.

Short bench session tonight, and a small one that I want on record because the multimeter underpins every current figure I give for the nodes. At 22:29 Tomasz mentioned that his Aneng AN8008 had a dim backlight and a blinking battery icon. I confirmed it uses a 9 V 6F22 battery and that the low-battery icon normally appears under about 7.2 V. He swapped in a fresh Duracell that had been in the drawer after the smoke detector change. The old battery read 6.9 V on the meter itself, so the warning was legitimate and the meter was not faulty. Backlight auto-off after about 15 seconds is a built-in behavior, not a setting, and he now knows that is normal.

Why this matters for the project: the AN8008's microamp and milliamp ranges are what we use for sleep-current figures, and a weak battery can make a handheld meter read slightly off or reset mid-measurement. I do not have any evidence that readings were off before tonight, so I am not discarding any past numbers. But when we do the next current measurement it is worth noting that the meter was on a fresh battery as of this date.

Things I would like to follow up on: ask next session how long the new battery lasts per the tape date, which gives a rough battery-life number for the meter in real use. Also worth considering a spare 9 V stored in the bench drawer next to the fuse spares so he does not have to dig for one. Tomasz said he was heading to bed around 23:10, so I kept the notes brief. Honest answer: not directly. A BME280 can't see clouds. A cheap proxy is a light sensor such as the Adafruit VEML7700 (0 to 120,000 lux, I2C address 0x10), where a slow morning ramp versus a jumpy one hints at broken cloud. Why self-heating is not a concern on the rooftop node: the BME280 is run in forced mode with 1x oversampling on all three channels, so each measurement takes about 8.2 ms typical per the datasheet and the part sleeps otherwise. At one reading every 300 s the active fraction is tiny. If he ever switches to normal mode with a 0.5 ms standby, that conclusion changes, and the datasheet's own application note warns about the temperature offset in that case. I should remind him of that before any firmware that changes the mode.

I2C speed: the rooftop node runs the ESP32 Wire default of 100 kHz. I confirmed with him that he never changed it. An 8-byte burst read is under a millisecond, so there is nothing to gain from fast mode, and a slower clock is more forgiving of longer cable runs and noisy rooftop wiring.

A flattened bead usually still reads fine for air, it just responds slower since there's more thermal mass touching the air stream. Give it 20 to 30 seconds to settle before you trust the number. The first topic was the flicker on Tomasz's clip-on desk lamp, a $9 IKEA unit with a 4 W LED bulb. It flickered whenever his soldering iron's heater switched on, about once every 2 seconds, matching the iron's heater indicator. My explanation was that a temperature-controlled iron pulses its heating element and the line voltage sags a little each time; a cheap LED driver with minimal input filtering shows that as visible flicker. He moved the lamp to the wall outlet behind the desk instead of the shared power strip, and the flicker went away. That confirms the strip was the shared path. I noted that sensitive gear such as the multimeter is better kept off that strip while the iron is running, though I have not heard of any actual measurement problems.

The second topic was wire length. He cut a nominal 30 cm piece of 22 AWG red wire and, after stripping, measured 29.4 cm. The 0.6 cm gap is the two 3 mm strips at the ends, which he recognized once I said it. My suggestion, for any pigtail where length matters inside an enclosure, is to measure the insulated length before stripping and label that number. I think this is worth remembering as a convention for his cable labels: the label should describe what you would measure with a ruler against the finished part.

Things I noticed about how he works: he tends to ask a small question just before closing the laptop and wants a one-line cause rather than a lesson. He ended the session quickly and cheerfully, so no open threads are hanging from this one.

Thursday August 13, late evening. Short session about a ticking fan on the Pi case, nothing to do with the sensor network, but worth keeping because Tomasz hears this thing from the couch and it will bother him until it is fixed.

What I know: the fan is a 30 mm unit in an Argon-style case, about 4 months old, powered from the header 5 V pin with a 2-pin lead and no PWM control. The sound is a tick roughly once per second, which does not fit a bearing fault. A bearing problem at 6,000 to 7,000 rpm would show up as a growl or buzz, not a slow tick. Candidate causes, in order of likelihood: the fan lead, which Tomasz says is looped right next to the hub; a lid that is not seated, since there is a 2.5 mm gap on one edge; and a standoff of the wrong height.

What I suggested: reroute the lead away from the blades and hold it with a 3 mm adhesive cable clip, which he thinks he has in the drawer with the heat shrink. Then tighten the four lid screws in a cross pattern a quarter turn at a time and see whether the gap closes to under 1 mm. Test after each change so we know which one fixed it, otherwise the next ticking noise will have no history.

The electrical side is fine. A fan like this pulls about 0.1 A, around 0.5 W, which is small against the supply he installed in July. I do not see any need to move the fan to a PWM pin or add a transistor.

Open items for next session: ask which fix worked, ask the final lid gap in millimetres, and ask whether the tick came back after a few hours of running. If the lid gap does not close, ask him to measure the standoff heights with calipers. I would also like to know whether the tick changes when the Pi is under load, because fan speed does not change on this wiring and the tick should not either. If it does change, then the cause is more likely vibration coupling from the drive shelf than the fan itself.

The first was a student's R script for the Lab 5 density table. The symptom was every group's mean density showing as 0.0. Densities of snow in this exercise should fall between roughly 0.35 and 0.60 g/cm³, so a column of zeros pointed to either type coercion or rounding. I suggested checking structure with str() before anything else, because a character column would have produced errors or NA rather than zeros, which made rounding more likely. The cause was round(density, 0), carried over from a snow water equivalent column where whole millimeters are sensible. I told Anjali the general lesson for the lab: digits in round() should match the precision of the instrument, and here the balance reads to 0.1 g on a 500 cm³ cutter, so three decimals is defensible and zero is not. I would consider a line in the grading notes saying that students who round to whole numbers lose no points for the method but should be asked to show unrounded values.

Sunday evening session with Tomasz, short and about the bench multimeter rather than the weather network. His Aneng AN8008 stopped reading on the mA range after he probed a 5 V rail with the red lead still in the mA jack. That is the classic way to take out the input fuse, and the meter itself is fine. I told him the fuse on this family of meters is normally a 500 mA fast-blow 5x20 mm glass tube on the mA/µA input and a separate 10 A fuse on the high-current jack, and I asked him to confirm against the label inside the battery cover instead of trusting my memory of the family. He has spares: a 10-pack of 500 mA fast-blow tubes that arrived with a March Mouser order. He confirmed the blown one reads open on continuity.

Why I care about this beyond the fix: the node work depends on current measurements. The sleep-current figures we have been estimating for the sensor nodes only mean something if the meter's mA and µA ranges are trustworthy, and a meter with a mismatched or oversized fuse is a risk to the shunt resistor and to him. I discouraged a higher-rated fuse for that reason. A fuse is cheap, a burned shunt is a dead meter.

What I recorded: a bench-notes line telling him to return the red lead to the VΩ jack after every current measurement, and the fuse spec. He is putting red P-touch tape beside the mA jack as a visual cue. I suggested a safe verification once the new fuse is in: a 9 V battery with a 1 kΩ series resistor should show about 9 mA, which exercises the range without any risk.

Open for next time: ask whether the new fuse is in and the 9 mA check read near 9 mA. If it reads noticeably off, the shunt or range calibration is worth a note before trusting any µA measurement of the ESP32 in deep sleep. Working note on how I keep this experiment honest. The pass criterion Tomasz and I agreed on is that the cone should be more open on at least 5 of 7 days when RH is below the weekly median. Two cautions I am keeping in the notes. First, a cone that opens when dry and closes when wet should widen with falling RH, but evening readings have been wider than morning ones on both days with data, and mornings are usually humid in Portland in spring. Only the 3.5 mm swing from Wednesday morning to Friday evening clears that bar.

Session note, Sunday March 1, evening. Tomasz came in with what looked like a dashboard bug: his wind Stat panel showed 3.9 m/s while the trees outside looked like more. It turned out not to be a bug but a sampling limit. The rooftop node takes a single 2 s anemometer sample per 300 s wake, so the stored value is a snapshot, and my first assumption that his query was averaging was wrong in detail, since there is nothing to average inside one window. I told him what the real fix would look like (a max-aggregated field), and we both agreed the panel label was the thing to change today. He renamed it to 'Wind snapshot (m/s)'.

The bigger thread is how to capture gusts without wrecking the power budget. I costed a 10 s sampling window and it nearly doubles his average current, which he rejected quickly. The alternative I proposed uses the ESP32 PCNT peripheral so the hardware does the counting while the CPU sleeps. I noted the glitch filter details so he doesn't have to dig through the technical reference manual: 80 MHz APB clock, so a 1000-cycle filter rejects pulses under 12.5 µs.

What I wrote into the anemometer project notes: PCNT unit 0, input GPIO 27, 3 s window read in 250 ms steps, store wind_max next to the mean. Open question for next time: whether GPIO 27 conflicts with anything on the spare board layout, and whether the pulse count in a 250 ms slot is large enough to give useful resolution. At the usual calibration of about 0.5 m/s per pulse per second, a single count in a 250 ms slot would mean 2 pulses/s granularity, so resolution may be coarse. I should work that out with him before he spends Tuesday on it.

Wednesday evening, January 28. Desmond came to me at 6:58 pm about a dripping kitchen faucet. It is a single-lever Delta that predates their 2004 purchase of the house, and the drip comes from the spout at roughly one drop every four seconds. He shut the water off under the sink at 6:40 pm and took the faucet apart himself before asking me much of anything, which is his habit and a good one. It is a ball-type model with a slotted cam cap. He found the two inlet seats hard and flattened, and one had a worn ring, so the diagnosis is plain: seats, and likely springs, are done.

What I advised: replace seats and springs as a pair, and pick up a new cam, packing and O-ring set while he is at it, because a ball faucet tends to weep from the body next if only the seats are done. He agreed, with the reasoning that he dislikes opening a faucet twice. I think that is the right instinct for a man who retired after thirty-one years of fixing other people's equipment and knows how often a half repair comes back.

He also mentioned that the hot-side shutoff under the sink is stiff. I told him not to force it. Old quarter-turn stops can have a packing nut that is dried out, and a hard turn can start a leak at the stem that is worse than the one he is fixing. He will work it gently with penetrating oil. If the stem weeps afterward, a quarter turn on the packing nut usually settles it. If the valve does not fully close, the water main shutoff in the basement is the fallback while he swaps parts.

For tomorrow I set a ping for 8:45 am to bag the old seats and carry the hex key. I will ask at supper time whether the drip has stopped and whether the hot side shuts off cleanly. I also want to remember, for the project list, that this faucet is over twenty-two years old, so a full replacement may come up before long, and he may prefer a model with a ceramic cartridge that is simpler to service.

Yep: run `vcgencmd get_throttled` on the Pi. It prints a hex bitmask, and 0x0 means no under-voltage or throttling has happened since boot. Bit 0 (0x1) is under-voltage right now, bit 2 (0x4) is currently throttled, and bit 18 (0x40000) means throttling has occurred at some point. A Pi 4 starts soft-throttling at 80 °C, so a warm case alone is fine.

Project note: Lab 7 teaching materials. Current state of the stage-discharge exercise as of the evening of October 9. The data file is rb_rating_14.csv, 14 stage/discharge pairs from the Red Butte Creek gauge, with a lowest stage of 0.21 m. The instructor script is lab7_rating_solution_v2.R. It fits Q = a(h - h0)^b with nls() using starting values a = 1, b = 2 and h0 set 0.05 m below the lowest observed stage. It then prints confidence intervals and draws a log-log residual plot.

Design decisions so far. First, students may use R or a spreadsheet, consistent with the flexibility Anjali has allowed in earlier labs, but the handout should say plainly that the starting value for h0 must be below the smallest stage. Second, the form of the curve follows Rantz et al. 1982. Third, the exponent should be reported to one decimal place, because with this few points the second decimal carries no information.

Working notes on small-scope hygiene, Jul 28. Today's patch was a 7-line redirect, and it shows a pattern in this repo: the cheap fixes come from reading Sentry, not from guessing. Sentry's 404 list is a free source of broken-link evidence. A weekly look at transactions with status 404, grouped by path, would take about 3 minutes and would have caught the old /appointments/list path in March, soon after the rename.

Two cautions. First, a permanent 301 gets cached by browsers. If the target route name changes again, those bookmarks will keep pointing to the old place until cache clears. That is acceptable here because the target is the stable appointment list. Second, the redirect pattern accepts an optional trailing slash. Django's APPEND_SLASH setting does not apply to a path that already matches a pattern, so both forms resolve and the test covers only the no-slash form. Adding the slash form to the test is about 1 minute.

Session note, Thursday evening, Tomasz. Main problem was the phone version of Grafana Explore timing out on a 90-day range query against the weather bucket with no aggregation. The laptop got through it, the phone did not, which says the query was marginal rather than broken. The cause is that Flux was asking the Pi for every raw point, roughly 25,900 per node over 90 days at the 5-minute post interval, and the data source Timeout field was blank. We added aggregateWindow with a 1-hour mean and createEmpty set to false, and set the data source timeout to 60 s as a safety net. The rooftop series now returns 2,159 points in 2.3 s on the phone. He noticed it was one short of my estimate of 2,160; I put that down to a partial bucket at the start of the window, which I think is right but have not verified by looking at the first timestamp. A small thing to check next time he has the query open: the earliest _time returned.

I want to keep a standing habit in these notes: any long-range panel starts from an aggregated query, and raw queries are reserved for ranges of a day or two. That keeps phone use responsive without anyone touching the Pi.
