Session note, Thursday September 3, 2026, 11:51 pm start. Anjali wrote late and in a hurry, as she often does, to propose a new fall lab: Lab 10, a potential evapotranspiration exercise using the Hargreaves-Samani equation. The data source is NOAA daily summaries for the Salt Lake City airport station. Each of the 9 groups will receive a different 7-day window from June to August 2025, which keeps the work independent without making the exercise long. I want to record the design decisions in one place so that the later prep sessions do not have to reconstruct them.

The equation. Anjali first had a coefficient of 0.0027 on scrap paper and then recalled 0.0023. I told her I believe 0.0023 is the standard form, and I flagged that as from memory. FAO-56 (Allen et al. 1998) is the reference I would check, and I have not yet verified the exact wording there. I also want to confirm how Ra is expressed, since the formula only works if Ra is in evaporation-equivalent mm/day, not MJ per square meter per day. A student who plugs in the wrong unit would get an answer off by a factor of roughly 2.45, and that is a plausible source of confusion on the day. The handout should print the unit next to the Ra column.

The worked row. With Tmax 31 C, Tmin 15 C and a placeholder Ra of 16.5 mm/day, I computed ET0 of about 6.19 mm/day, shown as 6.2. The Ra value is hers, not looked up, and remains a placeholder until I build a monthly table for roughly 40.8 N.

Open items I am carrying: verify the coefficient in FAO-56, build the Ra table by month, confirm that the NOAA export gives temperatures in Celsius or convert from Fahrenheit if it does not, and check whether any of the nine chosen weeks has missing days. The default NOAA daily product is often in Fahrenheit, so I expect a conversion step and will add a note on the sheet.

The file is lab10_pet_sheet_v1. Its columns are date, Tmax, Tmin, Tmean, range, Ra and ET0, with a weekly total row. I set a reminder for Monday September 7 at 10:50 am for the data pull.

Measured today for future reference. Local laptop, serial: 58s for 99 tests. Local with --parallel 4: 21s. CI total is a little over 4 minutes, and the test step is only a minority of that. That's the classic low-current auto-shutoff. Many banks cut output when the draw falls under roughly 50 to 100 mA, and a deep-sleeping ESP32 pulls around 10 µA on the chip but maybe 5 to 8 mA on a DevKit because of the CP2102 and the AMS1117 quiescent current. Look for a bank with a 'low-current mode' (usually a double-press of the button), or add a 100 Ω 1 W resistor across 5 V and GND to burn about 50 mA as a dummy load.

Saturday evening session, short and mostly about the reset path on the bench spare, the ESP32 DevKit labeled A. Tomasz wanted to know why pressing EN always reported rst:0x1, POWERON_RESET. I explained that EN drives the chip through the same reset route as a cold power-up on the classic ESP32, so the ROM cannot distinguish them. The useful tool is esp_reset_reason(), which reports the cause recorded by the chip: power-on, software restart, deep sleep wake, brownout, watchdog. He wired it into a switch statement that prints both the enum number and a name. Results on the bench: ESP_RST_POWERON after plugging in USB, and ESP_RST_SW after a deliberate esp_restart() triggered by a press on GPIO 0, the BOOT button. That is a clean confirmation that the logging works.

Why this matters for the nodes: once a node sleeps between readings, most boots will be ESP_RST_DEEPSLEEP, and anything else is interesting. A brownout reset on a battery node would be an early sign of a sagging cell under radio load, and a watchdog reset would point at a hang in the code. I suggested he eventually send the reset reason as a small integer field alongside the readings, so odd boots show up on the dashboard without anyone watching a serial monitor. He did not commit to that, and I left it as an idea in the project notes rather than a task.

He also asked about the 'ets Jun  8 2016 00:22:57' banner. That is the ROM bootloader's build stamp, the same on every classic ESP32, printed at 115200 baud on UART0 before user code runs. I noted a debugging tip: if the banner turns into garbage characters, the monitor baud rate is the first suspect, not the chip.

Open items for next time: whether he wants the reset reason stored, and whether the button-triggered restart test should be removed before the sketch is reused. Session ended around 21:15 as planned. PCNT bench test: Tomasz built a pulse driver out of the second spare ESP32, GPIO 33 into the counter board's GPIO 27 with a shared ground. At 10 Hz the counter read 30 or 31 over a 3 s window across five runs, which is the expected window-edge jitter of plus or minus one edge. At 200 Hz it read 598 of 600. I told him this was consistent with the unsynchronized windows, not with the glitch filter, because 2.5 ms pulses are far above the filter limit. The read loop is twelve vTaskDelay calls of 250 ms, so real elapsed time runs slightly past 3 s; the next step is logging esp_timer_get_time() at both ends and dividing counts by measured seconds.

What I still do not know is how fast the real anemometer pulses at high wind, and whether its reed contact bounces. That decides whether the 12.5 µs filter is even needed. I want his spec sheet or a pulses-per-revolution figure before we pick a final window length. A bench square wave is cleaner than a mechanical switch, so passing here proves the counter logic only.

Saturday March 7, evening session with Tomasz, about the daily temperature range panel for the rooftop station. I want to keep a few notes here that are not about the panel itself, because the panel went together quickly and the interesting part is what I learned about how he queries.

The thing that tripped him was day bucketing. aggregateWindow with every: 1d aligns to UTC midnight by default, so in Pacific winter the buckets begin at 4 pm local. A day's high and low then get split across two buckets, which compresses the apparent range. He noticed it because Thursday looked odd. I suggested the offset parameter and, in the future, I should check bucket alignment first whenever a daily aggregation looks off, before suspecting the sensor.

The two-query design, max and min with a subtraction transform, is something I would reuse for a wind gust panel later if he wants the spread between mean and peak. It avoids pivot() and keeps the Flux readable on the phone-sized editor, which matters because he often edits from the couch.

I also want to record a modelling point for later: diurnal range is a handy proxy for cloud cover. Overcast days shrink it, clear days widen it. If he ever wants a crude sky-condition indicator without a pyranometer, range plus the day's mean humidity would be a candidate, though I would not trust it without comparing against the airport observations for a few weeks.

Session note, Monday April 13, evening. Tomasz brought a small sysadmin question instead of a hardware one. His Pi's journal showed three ntpd-style 'TIME_ERROR 0x41 Clock Unsynchronized' lines around 03:12 on the morning of the 13th. By the time we looked, at 21:12 Pacific, timedatectl reported synchronized with offset +3.1 ms against a Cloudflare time server, poll interval 1024 s. I explained that the flag is the kernel's sync bit dropping briefly, likely after a DNS blip or daemon re-resolve, and that for 5-minute weather sampling this is harmless. My rule: only investigate if it recurs on 3 or more nights, and in that case check chronyc tracking and consider switching from timesyncd to chrony.

Two follow-ups I kept. First, a low-priority item to check the router's DHCP reservation for the host pi4, because the nodes depend on reaching it reliably. Tomasz did not know the lease time and I told him it matters little with a reservation. Second, I gave him a journalctl one-liner that counts priority-err messages per day over seven days, with a rough threshold of 50 per day as the point where I would start reading the logs. He has not run it yet, so I do not know his baseline.

Tomasz ran into the log by accident while grepping for his temperature script, which tells me the pi_health cron output is probably still the thing he checks most. Nothing was changed on the Pi tonight; it was read-only diagnosis. Open item for next time: ask whether the error count output looked normal, and whether the 03:12 message came back on the nights of the 14th and 15th.

On a personal note for the notes file, he sounded relaxed and was working from the couch rather than the bench.

What I would do differently: I should have asked up front for the full line of journal output including the process name, because 'ntpd' is unusual on a stock Raspberry Pi OS and might mean he installed it separately at some point. I'll ask next session which time daemon is actually running, since the advice differs slightly between timesyncd, chrony and ntpd.

Session note, Sunday October 11, 2026, about 9 pm. Anjali wrote from home and proposed a Lab 24 on open-channel flow using Manning's equation. I want to record how the arithmetic went, since it is the sort of thing a student will also trip over. She first gave the hydraulic radius for a 2.0 m wide, 0.5 m deep rectangular channel as 0.5, having divided 1.0 by 2.0. The area of 1.0 m2 is right, but the wetted perimeter needs both banks, 3.0 m, so R is 0.33 m. I suggested the lab keep that as a discussion point, because forgetting the side walls is a very common slip.

The design: two rows per group, one natural channel with n near 0.03 and one lined with n near 0.013. I flagged the n values as coming from memory of the Chow tables and marked them verify on the sheet. The worked row uses slope 0.002 and gives V of about 0.69 m/s, which I computed quickly; Anjali will redo it by hand Tuesday morning, which is the right check. I would not trust my mental exponent on R^(2/3) for the printed key until we have both numbers agreeing.

Open items: I do not know whether the concrete flume section she mentioned has a measured slope anywhere, so the 0.002 is invented for teaching. If a real reach is used, the sheet needs a surveyed slope. The sheet is lab24_manning_sheet_v1, one page, eight columns. Session note, Wednesday April 8, 18:17. Tomasz came in with the results of the first plume run on the bench spare, and this note is about how I want to treat that dataset and the Friday follow-up, not a replay of the chat.

What the bench run is good for: it proves the sketch works. The run produced 81 samples from 20:50 to 21:30, which is exactly the number I computed for a 30 s cadence, so there are no dropped wake cycles and no timing drift worth chasing. It does not prove or disprove the dryer-vent theory, because the spare sits on a shelf by a window indoors, a different air mass from the rooftop. The humidity bump there peaked at about 21:07 and was +1.9% RH, so I am labeling that run in the project notes as a sketch validation only. I would rather keep it from being mistaken later for plume evidence.

Plan for Friday April 10 around the 9 pm window. Tomasz will clip the spare near the mast bracket, with a jumper run of about 1.5 m. Constraints I gave him: at least 30 cm of separation from the rooftop sensor, its own power from a USB battery bank rather than the Pi, its own I2C bus so nothing collides, and the plume_test measurement with node_id tag bench_a so the production series stays untouched. Forecast he quoted is dry and about 11 °C at 9 pm, which is good because rain or fog would swamp a small humidity bump. If the spare shows a bump of roughly 3 to 5% RH near 21:05, that supports the vent. If it shows nothing while the rooftop node shows its bump, I will want to look at whether the rooftop box itself traps something, and that would be a different conversation.

Session note, Sunday July 12, about fall Lab 17 (stream cross-section at the Red Butte footbridge). Anjali opened with the idea at 1:09 pm and was relaxed about it, which is not her usual tone on a lab design. She wants students to stretch a tape across the channel and measure depth every 0.5 m, then compute area. Her recollection is that the creek is about 3 m wide at the footbridge, but she was explicit that this is a guess, so I recorded it as unverified. The prep list now carries three new items in this order: measure footbridge channel width, check closet for wading rod (resolved the same day), and later the data sheet draft.

The rod question resolved quickly. Dana sent a photo showing a plain fiberglass rod with centimeter marks, 1.2 m long, and no top-setting scale. Anjali had pictured a 1 m rod, and she did not want a bendable meter stick because the stick flexes in current. That detail matters for the sheet: the depth column should allow readings up to 1.2 m, though October depths in a small creek will probably be far less. I have not checked the gauge history yet, so I should not say anything about typical depth beyond that being my plan.

On method, we settled on midsection area. She remembered it only vaguely from her civil engineering coursework, so I wrote out the logic in plain terms for her: depth at a station times half the distance to each neighbor. With uniform 0.5 m spacing it simplifies to depth times 0.5 m for interior stations, which keeps the sheet to one computed column. I flagged that the bank stations would contribute near zero and that students may be confused about whether to include them. A footnote on the sheet may help.

Open items for next time: actual channel width, whether students can wade safely in October (water temperature and flow unchecked), how many wading rods per group, since the closet seems to hold only one, and whether Lab 17 fits the week order alongside Labs 13 to 15. Tomasz is building the hallway e-paper display on a perfboard carrier for spare ESP32 DevKit E, and tonight was about the 8-pin 2.54 mm female header that takes the Waveshare adapter plug. The first soldering pass left the strip tilted about 5 degrees, high at the pin 8 end, because he soldered pin 1 first and never tacked the opposite end. Session note, Saturday evening, Tomasz's Grafana cleanup on the phone layout.

This was a short, cosmetic session, but it fits a pattern I want to keep in the project notes: Tomasz is steadily tuning the dashboard for reading on his phone rather than a desktop browser, and each fix has been about how much space text takes on a 390 px wide screen.

What we changed tonight. The rooftop humidity Stat panel was showing two decimals, which clipped the value on the phone. He set Decimals to 0 on that panel, so it now reads as a whole percent. I suggested 1 decimal for the dew point panel, and his current reading there is 7.4 °C. The reasoning is that the BME280 humidity spec is about ±3% RH, and dew point is computed from humidity, so extra digits imply an accuracy we do not have. Display rounding does not touch what is stored in InfluxDB, which is worth remembering if we ever do derived calculations: they should use the raw field, not the displayed number.

The second change was the title size. Auto title sizing scales with panel width, and six-column panels end up with oversized titles on a narrow screen. Setting Text size > Title to 14 and leaving Value on auto gave him small labels and large digits, which is what he wanted. He saved the dashboard as version 23 with the message 'phone tidy pass', which is a good habit; if a later change breaks the layout we can diff against that version.

Things I would like to do next time, none urgent: apply the same title size to the pressure and temperature panels so the row looks consistent, and check that the title setting survives a JSON re-import. Notes on the Pi case question, June 21. Tomasz wondered aloud about swapping his plain black vent-free plastic Pi 4 case for a passive aluminum heatsink case, mentioning the Argon and Flirc names. He framed it as a casual idea after Priyanka asked whether the Pi makes noise. It does not; there is no fan.

My view, recorded so I stay consistent: a passive aluminum case commonly lowers Pi 4 temperatures by something like 10 to 15 °C under sustained load, costs roughly $15 to $25, and for a mostly idle box is a comfort upgrade rather than a necessity. The right first step is a baseline. I asked him to run vcgencmd measure_temp after a long Grafana session and write down the number, then compare after any change.

A caution I should raise when he does shop: confirm the case is made for the Pi 4 specifically, since the USB-C power port and the two micro-HDMI ports sit in different places than on older Pis. Also, some aluminum cases block the Wi-Fi antenna somewhat, so if the Pi ever moves off Ethernet that matters.

Nothing was decided or ordered. I am treating this as a low-priority idea and not adding it to the parts list unless he says so.

Planned for next time: ask whether he took the baseline temperature reading and what it was.

Project note: rooftop node reliability. Collecting what I know so the next session can pick it up cold. The rooftop node posts every 300 s over Wi-Fi to the Pi. Failures I have seen so far fall into two kinds: an isolated POST error (HTTP code -1) with the server healthy, and a three-post gap that coincides with an InfluxDB TSM compaction. Different causes, probably, so I should not lump them together in the notes.

Planned firmware changes, in order of effort: first, HTTP_TIMEOUT_MS from 3000 to 8000; second, log post_ms and retries as extra fields on each point; third, only if gaps continue, buffer the last two readings in RTC memory and send them together after a failed cycle, so a gap becomes a delayed point rather than a hole. The third option adds complexity and a risk of duplicate timestamps, so I will hold off until the data from the first two justifies it.

What I would like to learn from data: how long each post takes in normal operation (I expect well under 1 s), and whether slow posts cluster near compaction times. If they do, the fix is on the Pi side, not the node side.

My suggestion for Tomasz to try when the logs exist: a small query for the longest post_ms per hour over a week.

Probably not. Most of those meters resolve 0.01 A at best, and the display often rounds to 1 mA, so a 0.9 mA average will read as 0 or 1. Project note: anemometer firmware. Current state: sketch counts reed or Hall pulses in an ISR into a uint8_t over a 2 s window, then multiplies by 0.5 to get m/s, which is wrong by a factor of 2.5 relative to the intended 5 s window. Planned fix: define WINDOW_S as a constant, compute speed as pulses times the per-pulse factor divided by WINDOW_S, and widen the counter to uint16_t so a strong gust cannot wrap it. Before reflashing I want him to log raw pulse counts alongside speed for one evening, so the conversion can be audited later and not only the result.

Backfill idea: a Flux query that selects the wind field from the January change date forward and divides by 2.5 into a corrected measurement, rather than overwriting the original points. That keeps the raw history intact if the factor turns out to be slightly off. Conversion reference for comparisons: 1 knot is 0.5144 m/s, so a 9 kt airport reading is about 4.6 m/s.

Things I do not know yet: the exact date of the sampling change, and whether the node that reports wind has had any other edits since. I will ask in the next session.

Friday night bench session with Tomasz, 22:54. Today was about the PCNT edge counter on the second spare DOIT board, and I want to record the parts of the plan that aren't about the test numbers themselves. First, the shunt measurement method. He has a 10 ohm 1% through-hole resistor from the drawer and will measure the supply drop on his multimeter's mV range tomorrow morning. At 10 ohms the burden voltage is small, 10 mV per mA, but I should remind him that the ESP32 sees that drop as a lower supply, so the shunt must sit on the supply side of a regulated 3.3 V rail, never ahead of the USB 5 V feeding the dev board's regulator when the radio transmits, because the 120 to 160 mA bursts would drop 1.2 to 1.6 V across it and brown the chip out. The right place is the battery-side lead on a node running from a LiPo through its own regulator, and even then only in sleep-heavy tests. For the wake bursts, a much smaller shunt such as 1 ohm is the better choice. I will bring that up before he wires it. Second, the wind_max decision is closed: separate float field on the existing env measurement, written only when the PCNT window actually ran. I'll keep it out of the old history. Third, a note for the notes file: the PCNT counter work is finished at the bench level. Open items remaining are the light-sleep comparison and the pulses-per-revolution question for his actual anemometer, which I still haven't had answered. Friday 2026-02-20, evening. Tomasz came in wondering why the rooftop temperature panel always looked about five minutes stale with a one-minute dashboard refresh. The answer was the posting interval: the rooftop sketch sleeps 300 s between posts, and he pasted six timestamps that sat 5 minutes apart within a second of drift, with a spread of 1 s. The refresh rate is therefore not the limit, and he was fine with that once it was clear. The more useful discovery was a single missed post at 20:05. The InfluxDB health endpoint answered 200 and the service journal was clean for the window, so the server was not at fault. His node serial log showed an HTTP POST failure with code -1 at 20:05:04, which on the ESP32 HTTPClient means the connection was refused or could not be opened. My read is a transient Wi-Fi drop on the node side. I proposed a retry loop of 3 attempts with 2 s between them and a new integer field called retries, written with the next successful post, so that we can count how often the link stumbles over a week instead of guessing. I deliberately did not suggest shortening the cycle, because every extra wake costs battery on the remote nodes and the rooftop node should keep the same timing as the others for comparable data. Open items I am carrying: whether he adds the retries field to the rooftop sketch tonight or tomorrow, and whether the same failure shows up on the Sellwood node, which has a weaker signal path. I want a week of retries values before concluding anything about the Wi-Fi itself. If the count clusters at the same minute of the hour, I would suspect something periodic on the router, such as a scheduled channel scan, before blaming the node radio.

If the gap stays within 2 to 3 points across the hour, I will record it as a small offset note beside the bench spare entry. If the gap drifts, the likelier cause is temperature gradient between the two, because the Govee sits a few centimeters higher than the board.

The technical thread was a question about barometric pressure. He noticed that the rooftop BME280 showed a drop of 2 hPa between 14:00 and about 21:30 on a day the phone app called clear and dry. I explained the atmospheric tide: pressure has a twice-daily oscillation of roughly 1 hPa peak to peak at mid latitudes, with minima around 4 am and 4 pm local solar time, so part of what he saw is just the planet breathing. The rest is plausibly a slow synoptic change. The rule of thumb I gave him is that a fall of more than 3 hPa in 3 hours deserves attention, because that is the range where frontal systems start to show up in a station record. Below that, it is noise plus tide.

What I did not do tonight is verify any of it against his data, since I had no query result in front of me. So the claim that the dip is mostly tidal is a hypothesis, not a finding. Tomorrow morning I will compute the 3-hour pressure change across the last 24 hours and report the largest value, then compare it with whether any rain actually fell. If it turns out the tide explains the shape, I will suggest he subtract a fitted 12-hour sinusoid before building the tendency panel we discussed earlier, though that may be overkill for a hobby dashboard.

Monday night session, short and mostly about the network rather than the sensors. Tomasz said Grafana's home dashboard took about 6 seconds to open on the Pi. The 1.4 MB JS bundle was normal, so I suspected the link. His Wi-Fi was at 72.2 Mb/s and -67 dBm, which is a 20 MHz 802.11n rate with the Pi behind a bookshelf. He had a 2 m Cat5e cable left over from a game console. After plugging it in, ethtool reported 1000 Mb/s and the dashboard loaded in 1.9 s.

The interesting wrinkle was addressing. The Pi had a Wi-Fi address ending in .27, and plugging in Ethernet gave it a second interface with .42, which he reserved in the router for the Ethernet MAC. The nodes still post to the .27 address, so I advised leaving Wi-Fi up until the firmware is reflashed with the new one. I wrote that down as a loose end: do not disable wlan0 until every node posts to .42. One idea for later is to give the Pi a hostname through mDNS, such as the default raspberrypi.local, so the nodes never depend on a numeric address again. ESP32 mDNS lookups work but add roughly 100 to 300 ms at wake, which costs battery, so I would prefer a fixed IP plus a comment in the config.

Tomasz's phone kept opening Grafana at 'Last 6 hours' even though he believed he had saved 24 hours. The cause was the dashboard JSON model: the time block still carried "from": "now-6h", left over from an early version when he was only watching the rooftop node settle after a reflash. Grafana does not update that field unless the save dialog's checkbox for saving the current time range is ticked, and he had been changing the picker without ticking it. He edited the JSON directly to now-24h and saved the result as dashboard version 24 with the message 'default range 24h'. The phone now opens on the 24-hour view and the 1-minute refresh setting stayed as it was.

I also suggested capping max data points at 500 on the temperature panel. At a 5-minute cycle one node gives roughly 288 points in a day, so the cap does nothing today, but it protects the phone if he later widens the default range. He applied it. I did not recommend any change to the query itself, since the aggregation window is already set by the panel.

Something to remember for future dashboard work: when a setting seems to revert, check the JSON model before assuming the UI is broken, because the JSON is the source of truth after a save. If he re-imports a dashboard export, the time block comes back with whatever value the export held, so a quick look at it after any import is worthwhile.

Saturday April 4, late evening. Tomasz came in with a question that turned out to be a nice little piece of detective work: a recurring humidity bump on the rooftop station at about 9 pm. He first suspected the sensor. The data pointed elsewhere. Each bump lasted around ten minutes, with humidity up about 4.3% and temperature up 0.6 °C at the same time, starting near 21:05. A BME280 fault would not raise both channels in step with a plausible air parcel, and the humidity sensor's response time of about 1 s means it tracks a real plume faithfully. His partner's guess was the neighbor's dryer vent, and the 14-day query backed that up: 9 of 14 nights showed the event, with a gap on March 24 and 25. That irregular pattern looks like laundry habits, not electronics.

I also answered a self-heating question. In forced mode at 1x oversampling the chip is awake roughly 8 ms per wake, so any self-heating is negligible here. It would matter more in continuous normal mode at high oversampling.

What I did: put a Grafana annotation labeled 'dryer plume?' on the March 31 evening example so the pattern is documented where he looks every day. What I want to follow up: when the Sellwood data is next compared, check whether anything similar appears there. If it does at the same clock time, I would be wrong and the cause would be something shared, like the power supply or a scheduled job on the Pi. I think that is unlikely, but it costs one query to rule out. He stopped a little after ten and seemed content with the answer, which is the best outcome for a Saturday.

With the standard form C0 = (dt - 2KX) / (2K(1 - X) + dt): dt = 3 gives (3 - 4.8) / (19.2 + 3) = -1.8 / 22.2, so C0 = -0.0811. C1 = (dt + 2KX) / 22.2 = 7.8 / 22.2 = 0.3514, and C2 = (19.2 - 3) / 22.2 = 0.7297. They sum to 1.0000. The negative C0 is the thing to point students toward.

Session note, Thursday March 26, evening. Tomasz came in puzzled that his rooftop pressure panel showed 1016 hPa while his phone weather app said 1021 hPa for Portland. I explained the difference between station pressure and sea-level-reduced pressure. Weather apps and airport reports publish the reduced value, so a station sitting higher than sea level will always read lower. Near sea level the pressure falls about 12 hPa for every 100 m of height, which means a 5 hPa gap suggests roughly 40 m of elevation. Tomasz estimated his house at about 45 m on its hill in the west part of the city, which fits.

We decided to leave the raw pressure field alone in InfluxDB and compute a second field, pressure_msl, in Flux with a map() step. The correction uses 45 m as a constant. It adds about 5.3 hPa, and his panel now reads 1021.2 against the app's 1021. He retitled the panel 'Pressure (sea level, hPa)'. I reminded him that the BME280 datasheet specifies absolute pressure accuracy of about ±1 hPa, so the earlier 5 hPa gap could never have been sensor error, and the agreement within 0.1 hPa is partly luck given that accuracy figure. A single comparison is a sanity check, not a calibration.

Open items for me: his 45 m figure is an estimate from memory, so I want to check it against a terrain map or the phone's altitude reading before trusting the offset to the decimal. I will also compare his sea-level value against the app for several days and flag any gap that grows beyond 0.3 hPa, which would suggest either a wrong elevation or a drifting sensor. The same correction will eventually be needed for the Sellwood node, which sits at a much lower elevation, so it needs its own constant rather than reusing 45 m. Priyanka joked that the weather was now fake; Tomasz did not agree and neither do I.

Next time I should ask whether he wants the sea-level field in the Telegram alert text or only on the dashboard.

Here is a version of 14 lines: a function lh_pass(q, alpha) that loops once over the vector using f[i] = alpha*f[i-1] + (1+alpha)/2*(q[i]-q[i-1]), clips negative quickflow to zero, and returns q minus f. A wrapper lh_bfi(q, alpha = 0.925) applies forward, backward and forward passes and returns sum(baseflow)/sum(q). I saved it as lab12_lh.R. Anjali said yes as long as the table itself is turned in. I think that is a sound policy and I recorded it as a rubric line: any software is allowed, but units and the cutter volume must be visible. One risk is that a student who copies the old 1000 cm³ figure from last year's materials could carry the mistake through a script unnoticed, so the cutter-volume line on the worksheet matters more than before. Session note, Wednesday April 15, evening. Tomasz brought a wind panel puzzle: the rooftop mean wind line sat at exactly 0.0 m/s from 14:10 to 14:35 while wind_max for the same period read 3.1 m/s. With a fresh 500 mA fast-blow fuse in the Aneng AN8008 and a 9 V battery through a 1 kΩ resistor, the mA range read 8.7 mA, against 9 mA expected from Ohm's law. That is about 3% low, which a tired 9 V battery (probably sitting near 8.8 V under load) and a 5% resistor explain completely. The new topic was a spare ESP32 DevKit whose AMS1117-3.3 regulator tab measured 61 °C on his IR thermometer after 10 minutes of a WiFi scan loop. I worked out the dissipation: the regulator drops about 1.7 V from the 5 V USB input, and the scan loop peaks around 240 mA, so the instantaneous loss is about 0.4 W. A SOT-223 package with little copper can reach 60 °C at that level. That is within spec, since the junction limit is 125 °C, so I told him it is not a fault. The practical lesson for the project is that this heat only matters on the bench; the field nodes spend nearly all their time in deep sleep.

He also saw intermittent 'Brownout detector was triggered' messages, roughly 20 reboots earlier in the day. He added a 100 µF electrolytic across 3V3 and GND on the breadboard, and the messages stopped during the short test afterward. I think the cause is transmit current spikes sagging the rail, possibly made worse by a long thin USB cable. I suggested 470 µF as the next step and a shorter, thicker cable if the messages return.

He plans to leave the scan loop running overnight with a reset counter stored in RTC memory that prints on every boot, so he can read one number instead of scrolling the log. He expects to go to bed about 23:15.

Open items for next session: ask what the overnight reset count was; ask whether the 100 µF cap was enough or whether the 470 µF is needed; note in the bench file that the DevKit's regulator runs warm under WiFi load and that this is expected.

Session note, Friday April 10, evening. Anjali worked from her office until a little after 7:30 pm, mainly on the Lab 19 rating curve exercise. The main substance was the dataset itself. She had remembered the highest stage in the eight-point Red Butte Creek table as 1.2 m, but on checking the sheet it is 0.94 m, with the lowest at 0.21 m. I have changed the plotting limits in lab19_rating.R to a 0 to 1.0 m stage axis and will let the discharge axis follow the largest tabulated Q. I also want the handout to say plainly that the fit should not be extrapolated above 0.94 m, because a power law with a fitted offset can behave very differently outside the calibrated range.

We settled the number of points: I recommended keeping eight rather than ten. I proposed two panels, one in linear axes and one in log-log space after subtracting the fitted h0, so the offset is not hidden from students. I have not tested how nls behaves if students start from a poor h0 guess, and that is the next check I would run: try h0 at 0.0 m and at 0.20 m and see whether convergence fails, since the lowest stage is 0.21 m and h - h0 would be nearly zero there.

Method I am using: ingredient cost per gallon, then per cup at 16 cups a gallon, then compare to the $5.25 cup price. For the roasted red pepper soup, 12 lb of peppers cost $29.88, which is $7.47 per gallon across 4 gallons just for the peppers, about $0.47 a cup. A rule of thumb I am proposing: if the headline ingredient is under 10% of the cup price, no need to check anything else. If it passes 15%, I flag it before purchase. Gus did not object but also did not adopt it, so it stays a suggestion.

I will not apply this retroactively to older soups. Going forward I will log the headline ingredient cost for each new soup in one line so there is a short history by the end of winter.

Sunday evening session, short and mostly about the bench multimeter. Tomasz's handheld meter, which the cat pushed off the shelf, showed 0.4 mV on the 200 mV range with the probes shorted. I walked him through the fact that this is lead and contact offset rather than damage, and he found the REL button, which zeroed the reading to 0.0 mV. I want this written down because a lot of the measurements we plan involve tiny voltages: the shunt-resistor current measurements across a 10 ohm or 1 ohm resistor give only a few millivolts at the low currents, so a 0.4 mV offset would have been a real error. At 10 mV per mA across the 10 ohm shunt, 0.4 mV is 0.04 mA, which is about 4% of a 0.9 mA average, so zeroing first matters. After zeroing he measured the bench spare's 3.3 V rail at 3.28 V, output of an AMS1117-3.3 regulator. That is a decent baseline. If a later reading under radio load drops well below it, say under 3.0 V, that points to the input capacitor or the USB supply rather than the ESP32 itself, since the default brownout threshold is around 2.43 V. I noted that the bench spare's regulator has now been checked once and no action is needed. The cat remains the biggest hazard on the bench. Tomasz put Kapton tape along the shelf edge; I suggested a cardboard lip as a cheap alternative and expect neither to work. Open items for next time: remember to press REL before any millivolt-range reading, and, if we do the shunt test, record the zero offset in the project notes next to the result so a reader can tell whether it was subtracted. Anjali made the warm-up trim of 30 days an optional 1-point bonus. Session note, sunrise_proxy project, Wednesday July 22. Tomasz logged his second morning observation and it was a clean contrast with the first. On July 21 the rooftop at 05:30 read 14.6 °C with a 2.3 °C dew point spread and he scored the sunrise 7 out of 10 with some pink streaks. On July 22 the reading was 13.9 °C and 91% RH, the spread worked out to 1.4 °C, and the window showed solid gray, which he scored 2. That is the direction the 2 °C fog-or-low-cloud proxy predicts, so both days sit on the expected side, though I do not want to read anything into two rows. I want at least 10 mornings before fitting anything. I recorded the row in the table with the columns date, spread_c, pressure_hpa, trend_3h_hpa, score_0_10. Tomasz also mentioned that his window faces roughly east-northeast and that low cloud near the horizon likely matters more than overhead cloud. That suggests a useful extra column: a simple horizon cloud note in text, such as clear, thin streaks, or solid deck, written from the window rather than inferred from sensors. A text field is cheap and gives me something to cross-check the numeric proxy against. I also noted a side observation from the evening: the rooftop anemometer averaged 0.6 m/s between 6 and 8 pm, consistent with the calm he felt on a bike ride near the Springwater Corridor trailhead. I would like to see whether calm evenings tend to precede foggier mornings, since light wind lets surface air cool toward its dew point overnight. That is a hypothesis only. Next steps: keep the 05:30 pull consistent, add the horizon_note column when he is ready, and check after the fifth row whether the spread and score are moving together at all. Also confirm his new 5:20 alarm is holding, since a routine that costs sleep tends not to last.

Working note on data-processing conventions, written after the Brighton discussion on 2025-09-07. I am keeping this separate from the session note because it is meant to be read by whoever picks up the code next.

Timestamps: Brighton SNOTEL files in Anjali's folder use hourly top-of-hour stamps. USGS gauge files use 15-minute stamps. Any join between them should resample the gauge to hourly means first, not interpolate the SNOTEL series up to 15 minutes.

Snowfall estimate: function snowfall_from_pillow takes a daily SWE series in mm, takes the day-to-day difference, and keeps positive values only for November through April. Negative differences are left out of the snowfall total and logged separately as possible melt, settling or sublimation. I have not yet decided how to handle tiny positive increments below about 2 mm, which may be sensor noise; I plan to look at the distribution of increments at Brighton before choosing a threshold, and I will not pick a number until I see it.

Cross-check values recorded for Brighton, water year 2023: pillow increments 1,412 mm, gauge accumulation 1,538 mm. The gauge reads about 9 percent higher. The literature I would point to for gauge undercatch and pillow bridging is Fassnacht 2004, though neither explains a gauge reading higher than the pillow, so the gap may come from pillow losses to sublimation and wind redistribution. That is a hypothesis, not a finding.

Session note, Thursday October 9, 6:50 pm. Anjali came in with a narrow technical problem: an R script for the Lab 7 stage-discharge exercise returned NA for the rating-curve exponent. The cause was the nls() starting value for the datum offset h0. She had copied 0.25 m from an example written for a different creek, while the lowest observed stage in rb_rating_14.csv is 0.21 m, so the term (h - h0) went negative for the lowest points and the power produced NaN. I want to remember this failure pattern because it will recur for her students, many of whom will use R or Excel Solver with copied starting values. A good habit to teach is to compute min(stage) before fitting and to start h0 a few centimeters below it.

After she moved h0 to 0.16 the fit converged on the 14 pairs. I did not store the coefficients as results, since 14 points is thin and she said so herself. I treat the fit as a teaching example only. If she ever uses a rating curve in the dissertation, it should come from USGS data and not from this exercise.

I added two things to the instructor solution, now lab7_rating_solution_v2.R: a confint() call, because the interval on h0 is likely wide and students should see that, and a log-log residual plot, which shows systematic curvature if a single power law is the wrong form. I suggested an extrapolation question for next time, asking students to extend the curve to 2.5 times the highest observed stage and discuss why that is risky. I have not yet checked whether the Lab 7 time budget allows it.

She caught it herself when rereading the syllabus. I built lab6_rescale.csv, a 16-row lookup from 0 to 15 onto 0 to 12, rounded to the nearest half point. Proportional rescaling preserves percentages up to rounding error of at most 0.25 points, and I wrote that into the announcement discussion so it is not a surprise later. The Canvas announcement went up at 8:52 pm.

Saturday August 1, evening. Tomasz renamed the bench-room Raspberry Pi from the default hostname 'raspberrypi' to 'stratus', mostly because Grafana screenshots showed the old name in the footer. I want to record how it went and what I checked, since a hostname change is the sort of small edit that causes confusing failures weeks later.

Before the change we grepped /etc and the home directory for the old name. Three places turned up: /etc/hosts line 6, /etc/hostname, and a hard-coded MQTT_HOST of raspberrypi.local in the rooftop ESP32 sketch. The Sellwood node uses a fixed IP address, so it was unaffected. That is one more argument for the fixed-IP approach on remote nodes: they do not depend on mDNS resolving, which can be flaky on some routers.

We used the raspi-config non-interactive hostname command so both files change together. After the reboot, which took 27 seconds to login, stratus.local answered ping at 2.1 ms from Tomasz's laptop. The rooftop node was reflashed at about 18:52 and came back reporting with last-seen under a minute. The Grafana Telegram contact point message template also carried the old name in its title; that is now 'stratus alert'.

Things I want to watch. First, any cron script or note that references the old hostname in a path or log label; the grep found none, but scripts that build names dynamically would not show up. Second, whether the rooftop node reconnects correctly after a power cut, since mDNS has to resolve cold on boot. If it ever fails, the fallback is to give the Pi a DHCP reservation on the router and use the IP in the sketch, as Sellwood does.

Tomasz liked that Priyanka pointed out stratus is a cloud type. I have filed the new hostname under the Pi configuration notes. No open items remain from this change, but I will check the next day's rooftop uptime to be sure the reconnect holds.

Session note, Thursday July 16, evening. Tomasz came in with a power problem on the bench Raspberry Pi 4: the lightning-bolt under-voltage icon on the desktop and a vcgencmd get_throttled value of 0x50005. I decoded the bits for him: the low nibble says under-voltage and throttling were happening at that moment, and the 0x50000 part says both had also occurred since boot. The supply chain was an old 5 V 2 A barrel brick with a barrel-to-USB-C adapter and a P50 thin cable, which is a plausible cause on its own. The Pi is happy only if the voltage at its test pads stays above roughly 4.75 V under load, and that chain was very likely dropping several tenths of a volt once the CPU got busy.

He swapped to the official 15.3 W Raspberry Pi USB-C supply at 18:52, rebooted, and the flag read 0x0. I liked that he went on to measure instead of trusting the icon: 5.12 V at TP1 and TP2 with the Aneng multimeter while stress-ng ran on four cores. That gives a real number to compare against later if the icon ever comes back.

What I think is worth keeping from this: the symptom looked like a software or SD card problem at first glance, but the throttle register is the quickest way to rule out power. Next time any Pi misbehaves, check get_throttled before anything else.

Open items for next session: confirm the flag is still 0x0 after a full night of uptime, confirm the retired brick got its red NOT PI tape flag, and see whether he added the throttled string field to pi_health.sh. If he did, build a Grafana state timeline panel for it. I would also like to know whether the Pi was ever throttled during the earlier stress tests, because those temperature numbers might have been affected, though the earlier peak figures look consistent with thermal behavior alone.

Session note, Monday 2026-02-23, evening. Tomasz wanted the node status table on the dashboard to show last_seen as a human age instead of an epoch number. The fix was simple: set the column unit to Datetime from Now, which wants milliseconds, and his value 1771898702000 was already in milliseconds, so no multiplication was needed.

The interesting part was the confusion afterward. He saw two rows both labeled rooftop with different ages, 3 and 4 minutes, and briefly thought the bench spare was posting. It is not; it sits on a shelf with masking tape on it. The real cause was that his Flux query used last() without grouping, so the table got one row per field series, temperature and humidity, each with its own last timestamp. The two humidity and temperature points land a few hundred milliseconds apart in the write, and the table rounded them differently. Adding group(columns: ["node_id"]) before last() collapsed them into one row per node. I want to remember this pattern, because it will bite again when more nodes report: any status table built from last() needs an explicit group on node_id, otherwise the row count equals nodes times fields.

I suggested threshold colors on last_seen based on the 300 s post cycle. Green below 6 minutes gives one cycle of slack for jitter. Red at 11 minutes means two consecutive posts missed, which is the point where I would actually look at the node. I deliberately left out a yellow band because normal retry delays would make it flicker. Tomasz agreed.

He is also hiding the _start column with an Organize fields transform. Small cleanup, but it makes the table fit on a phone screen better.

Open items for next time: add a battery_mv column once nodes report it, and consider sorting the table by last_seen ascending so the stalest node is on top. Priyanka's reaction was that it looks like mission control, which is probably why he will not let me remove it later.

Sunday 12 April, evening session. Short and tidy: Tomasz's 'Last updated' tile on the rooftop dashboard was displaying a stale-looking timestamp, 2026-04-11 20:05, while data was arriving normally. The cause was a Flux query ending in |> first() instead of |> last(), which returns the oldest point in the 24-hour window rather than the newest. I explained that first() on a range of -24h will always land about a day back, and that is exactly the symptom he saw. He replaced it with last() and added group() ahead of it so a stray tag difference can never split the result into several rows. The tile then showed 20:45, one point behind the 20:50 wake that was still to come, consistent with the 5-minute cadence.

He also changed the unit to 'Datetime from now' so the tile reads as a relative age. Dashboard saved as version 28 with the message 'last updated tile fix'. I offered a staleness color scheme, amber after 15 minutes and red after 30, which would need a second query computing now() minus _time in seconds because the relative-time unit hides the raw number. Session note, Wednesday March 4, late evening. Tomasz finished the PCNT bench validation for the future anemometer sampler. The first 60 s run at 200 Hz came back 6 counts short of the nominal 12,000, and I had set a pass tolerance of 5, so on a strict reading it failed. I said so rather than rounding it into a pass. We then logged real elapsed time and found the window was 60.031 s, which moved the expected count to 12,006 and left a 12 count gap. My hypothesis was that the driver ESP32 was the slow party, because a pulse train built from vTaskDelay is quantized to the 1 ms FreeRTOS tick. Tomasz swapped the driver to the LEDC peripheral on GPIO 33, 8-bit duty resolution, 50 percent duty, and the next 60 s run matched exactly, 12,006 of 12,006. That isolates the error to the stimulus and clears the PCNT unit 0 configuration on GPIO 27.

Lessons worth keeping: always compute expected counts from measured elapsed time, not from the nominal window, and never generate a reference frequency from a software delay when a hardware timer is available. Next test is a 4 Hz and a 20 Hz drive over the 3 s window, expecting about 12 and 60 rising edges, with a plus or minus 1 tolerance on the low case. Tomasz plans it for Friday after work.

Also, his scratch folder had no version control. He created a repository, committed with the message 'pcnt bench test, LEDC driver', and added a .gitignore and a 4 line README covering the wiring. I want that wiring note to stay current if he moves pins.

Project note, rooftop station data quality, April 4. I want to keep a short list of known non-sensor effects on the rooftop readings so I stop treating them as mysteries. First on the list is the evening exhaust plume near 21:05: about +0.6 °C and +4.3% RH for ten minutes, seen on 9 of the last 14 nights, probably a neighbor's dryer. I recommended we keep it in the data and annotate it instead of filtering.

Second, the BME280 temperature accuracy of about ±1 °C means absolute values are less trustworthy than changes, and a 0.6 °C bump is still a meaningful change because the sensor's resolution is 0.01 °C. Third, the humidity channel's response time of about 1 s means short events show up cleanly at one reading per five minutes only if they happen to straddle a wake. Tomasz's wake cycle is 5 minutes and the plume lasts about 10, so at most two readings land in it. That is why the shape in the panel looks like a two-point blip and not a smooth curve. Worth remembering if he ever wants to characterize it: he would need a faster temporary logging interval for one evening, say every 30 seconds from 20:50 to 21:30, which on the bench spare would cost nothing since it runs on USB.

Session note, Wednesday July 15, late evening. Tomasz finished the saturated salt test of his spare bench BME280. The sensor sat in a sealed jar of NaCl slurry from Monday 22:10 to tonight and read 71.9% RH at roughly 23 °C. The expected value for NaCl at that temperature is about 75.4%, so the spare reads about 3.5 points low, just outside the datasheet's plus or minus 3% figure. I told him not to apply a correction to the rooftop humidity, because the rooftop board is a separate part and could be off by a different amount, or none. What I would be correcting is a single sensor with a single reading, and that is thin evidence.

Things I want to keep straight about the test. The jar was on a bookshelf, so it saw ordinary room temperature swings, and humidity above a salt slurry moves only slightly with temperature, but the 23 °C figure came from his room thermometer, not from the BME280's own temperature channel. I should ask him to log both next time. He also sealed the lid seam with a 1 cm strip of blue painter's tape as a tamper check. I suggested a second jar with silicone grease on the rim and magnesium chloride, which holds about 33% RH, giving him a low-end calibration point that matches the dry summer afternoons on the roof. He plans to look for MgCl2 sold as bath flakes at a pharmacy.

The outside comparison is a separate puzzle. His phone app said 45% on Sunday afternoon while the rooftop read about 38%. The app most likely draws from the Portland airport station, roughly 10 km away, so the gap is only partly a sensor matter.

Session note, Sunday 2025-09-07, late evening. Anjali spent this session on the Brighton SNOTEL record, specifically how to get snowfall out of a station whose precipitation gauge and snow pillow disagree on timing. She found a case on 2023-11-14 where the pillow rose 18 mm while the gauge read zero, and the gauge caught up two days later with 21 mm. My reading is that this is a reporting lag, not a failed gauge, though one event is thin evidence and I said so.

We settled on a working rule: for the snow season, November through April, estimate snowfall from positive daily pillow increments and keep the gauge as a cross-check. The check she ran for water year 2023 gave 1,412 mm from the pillow and 1,538 mm from the gauge, about 9 percent apart. That is inside the 10 percent tolerance I proposed, though I should be honest that the tolerance was a rule of thumb and not drawn from a paper. I would like to repeat the comparison for at least two other water years before the rule goes into a chapter, because 2023 was a large snow year and the ratio could behave differently in a thin one.

I wrote the rule into the processing log as a function named snowfall_from_pillow. Next checks I suggested: run it on Atwater and Alta-Collins for the same water year, and flag any day where the pillow drops while the gauge rises, which would mark rain-on-snow for the spring logic.

Small point for future me: Anjali briefly misremembered the Brighton reporting interval as quarter past the hour. The file shows top-of-hour stamps; the 15-minute stamps are the USGS gauge. I logged both so the join step does not mix them up.

Working note on the dashboard pressure panels, kept for later reference. Current configuration: the sea-level panel shows hPa; the tendency Stat panel uses a 3 h window with a 15-minute median pre-filter. Threshold colors are green below 1.6 hPa of absolute change and orange at or above. Direction is rendered by a text mapping, not by the threshold. Design reasoning: the smoothing window of 15 minutes is a trade between suppressing sensor jitter of about 0.3 hPa and reacting to genuine fast fronts. If a front drops pressure by more than 3 hPa an hour, a 15-minute median will lag by roughly one window, which is acceptable for a hobby display but would not be for alerting. Should Tomasz later want a Telegram alert on rapid falls, I would compute the tendency without the median and add a short pending period instead. Another idea for later: show the three-hour tendency beside a small history sparkline over 24 hours so the trend shape is visible, since a single number hides whether the drop was steady or sudden. Nothing here needs parts or budget.

Thursday May 21, evening session. Build night was cancelled because of a water leak at the makerspace, so Tomasz worked at home and brought me an under-voltage problem on the Pi 4.

What we saw: dmesg had a line 'hwmon hwmon1: Undervoltage detected!' timestamped Wednesday May 20 at 23:51:07. vcgencmd get_throttled returned 0x50000 when he ran it on Thursday evening. Bit 16 means under-voltage has occurred since boot and bit 18 means throttling has occurred since boot. The current-state bits, 0 and 2, are clear, so nothing is wrong right now. This differs from the 0x0 he got in April, so something changed in his setup. His space heater was running in the same room around the time of the event, which is my leading suspect for a mains sag.

The hardware: the charger is a generic one labeled 5 V 2.1 A, and the cable is a 1.5 m braided lead of unknown origin. The Pi 4 wants 5.1 V at 3 A officially. Idle draw is modest, but InfluxDB and Grafana plus the wifi radio create bursts, and a long thin cable adds a voltage drop through its conductors. I could not rule out the cable or the charger from his description alone.

What he did: clean shutdown, then he swapped in a 0.5 m USB-C cable from his drawer at 21:05. The Pi booted in roughly 50 seconds and Grafana came back without help. dmesg was clean right after boot.

My plan, with no decision made yet on buying anything: check dmesg for new voltage lines tomorrow morning, noting whether the heater was on. If the flag returns with the short cable, test with the heater off. If it still returns, the charger is the cause and a 5.1 V 3 A supply goes on the wish list, though I should flag that any purchase counts against his monthly parts allowance. I would also like him to add the get_throttled value to the pi_health cron at some point, though he declined that in April, so I will only mention it if the problem recurs.

Working notes on dashboard conventions, written after the legend cleanup on April 2. I want a short rule set the next session can lean on. First, display names should come from labels, not from hand-typed text, so ${__field.labels.node_id} is preferred over typing rooftop into an override; new nodes then label themselves the moment they report. Follow-up thoughts for my own notes, written after the session closed. These are small technical observations that came to mind and that I did not say to Tomasz, so I am recording them rather than losing them.

On desiccant in a sealed enclosure: a sealed box with a packet inside only helps if the box was dry when it was closed. If he seals it on a humid afternoon, the trapped air carries the moisture with it, and a 5 g packet will absorb part of that and then sit at equilibrium. For a spare enclosure sitting on a shelf this is fine, but for any deployed node it would be better to close the lid on a dry day and add a single packet, not rely on it as a cure for a leaky seal. A BME280 inside a box with a packet will also read lower humidity than the outside air, so any node using that trick should not be used as a humidity reference. I would mention this if he ever proposes it for a deployed node.

On the USB-C plug: a bent shell can also deform the internal contact springs of the receptacle on the board if it is forced in. If the board's port ever feels loose after this cable, that is the likely cause, and the fix is a different cable, not rework on the board.

On the grinder: hand grinders with burr sets often have a click-to-micron mapping that is roughly linear for a few steps. Three clicks is a meaningful jump, so going from 15 to 14 is a small and sensible move. I will keep any future coffee advice to one variable at a time.
